|
---
# **Taos Concert**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=5&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb spent the afternoon at Desert Rhythms in Taos, enjoying live music with families and neighbors. It was a great reminder that some of the best parts of life in New Mexico are free and meant to be shared. Deb will keep supporting the public spaces, local artists, and community events that make towns across our state such great places to call home.
---
|
---
# **Bean Day Parade**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=6&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
From the parade to the famous beans and barbecue, Bean Day is a reminder of the history, people, and traditions that keep small towns in New Mexico like Wagon Mound going strong. Deb had a wonderful time joining the 116th celebration of a tradition that has grown into a Labor Day homecoming for generations of New Mexicans.
---
|
---
# **Albuquerque Health Care for the Homeless**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=7&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb visited Albuquerque’s Health Care for the Homeless to learn more about their work connecting unhoused New Mexicans with healthcare and essential support. Meeting people where they are can make all the difference. As governor, Deb will invest in programs that make healthcare more accessible and ensure every New Mexican can get the care and support they need.
---
|
---
# **Maria Hughes Elementary School**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=8&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Universal childcare means more kids have a safe, supportive place to go after school while parents have peace of mind knowing their children are cared for. Deb visited a Boys & Girls Club of Central New Mexico to see how increased state funding is helping expand programs and reach more New Mexico families. As governor, Deb will keep building on that progress and investing in New Mexico’s families and future.
---
|
---
# **DPNM Rising Stars**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=9&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
The Democratic Party of New Mexico recognized two young leaders who are stepping up to serve our state. Deb was honored to celebrate Juan Sanchez and Amanda López Askin and their campaigns for Commissioner of Public Lands and Secretary of State. Deb is excited to work alongside a new generation of leaders bringing fresh ideas and a commitment to building an even better future for New Mexico.
---
|
---
# **State Fair Parade**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=10&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
New Mexico knows how to put on a fair! Deb had a great time supporting the New Mexico State Fair Parade. From Navajo tacos to turkey legs, there was no shortage of good food or good times at the fair. Deb is looking forward to many more days like this, celebrating New Mexico and meeting the people who make it special.
---
|
---
# **Ro Khanna and Gabe Vasquez Canvass Launch**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=11&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Congressmen Ro Khanna and Gabe Vasquez joined Deb in the South Valley to talk directly with voters. Deb knows how important knocking on doors, listening to people about what matters to them, and earning their support one conversation at a time. With strong organizing and people showing up, we can elect Democrats up and down the ballot this November.
---
|
---
# **Maravilla Gala**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=12&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
The Maravilla Gala was a wonderful way to kick off Hispanic Heritage Month and celebrate the culture and history that make New Mexico unique. Deb was grateful to the National Hispanic Cultural Center Foundation for creating space for Hispanic, Chicano, and Latino artists to share their work and for keeping these stories at the heart of New Mexico.
---
|
---
# **All for New Mexico Rally**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=13&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Gabe Vasquez and Pete Buttigieg joined Deb in Las Cruces to rally voters and get New Mexico ready for November. Southern New Mexicans know what’s at stake, and Deb was proud to see so many people ready to organize, talk to their neighbors, and turn out to vote. Deb is ready to bring that same energy and commitment to Southern New Mexico as governor.
---
|
---
# **Press Conference: Moratorium on New Data Centers Until Clear, Transparent Accountability Measures Are in Place**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=14&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb has spent her career fighting to protect New Mexico’s water, land, and communities, and she’s not backing down now. At her data center accountability policy announcement, Deb reaffirmed her support for a moratorium on new data centers until clear, transparent accountability measures are in place. New Mexicans deserve a say in how our water and other limited resources are used, and Deb will make sure that voice is heard.
---
|
---
# **Casakids**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=15&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb visited Casakids in Roswell to learn more about the team working to protect children and strengthen families across Southeast New Mexico. From advocacy to family services, Casakids helps children navigate difficult circumstances while making sure they’re not facing them alone. Children are our future, and Deb will make sure they have the resources they need to reach their full potential.
---
|
---
# **With Many Hands**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=16&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb toured a new project built by With Many Hands in Roswell to learn more about their work turning vacant and aging homes into affordable places for families to live. Their Rehab2Rental program is putting neglected properties back to use while creating more affordable housing in Southeast New Mexico. Deb knows New Mexico needs more affordable homes, and she’ll work with organizations like this to cut the red tape that keeps families from finding a place to call home.
---
|
---
# **Youth Development Incorporated**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=17&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb visited Youth Development, Inc. in Carlsbad to learn more about how their early childhood programs are helping New Mexico kids get a strong start. YDI pairs early education with health, nutrition, and family services, helping parents and children access the resources they need. With programs now reaching families across Eddy and Chaves Counties, Deb will build on this work as governor by expanding access to early childhood care and making sure rural families aren’t left behind.
---
|
---
# **North American Wind Research and Training Center**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=18&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb toured the North American Wind Research and Training Center at Mesalands Community College in Tucumcari to see how students are getting hands-on training for careers in the growing wind energy industry. New Mexico has an opportunity to turn our natural resources into good jobs while bringing new economic opportunities to rural communities. As governor, Deb will invest in workforce training and renewable energy to help New Mexico lead the way in the clean energy economy.
---
|
---
# **Portales Kick Ass Barn Party**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=19&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb had a great time at the Kick Ass Barn Party in Portales! Good food, great company, and a whole lot of energy from New Mexicans who are fired up about the future of our state. With early voting already begun, Deb is ready to keep the momentum going and elect Democrats up and down the ballot this November.
---
|
---
# **Child & Consumer Protections Press Conference**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=20&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb Haaland, Attorney General Raúl Torrez, and State Representative Linda Serrato (HD-45) announced their support for legislation developed by the Attorney General and to be sponsored by Rep. Serrato that puts New Mexico children first. The bills would strengthen protections for children online and give consumers more tools to stand up to corporate practices that put profits ahead of people. As governor, Deb will work with leaders across New Mexico to get these protections across the finish line and make sure families come first.
---
|
---
# **New Mexico Association for Home & Hospice Care**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=21&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb met with the New Mexico Association for Home & Hospice Care to hear about the challenges facing New Mexicans who rely on care at home. She sat down with Ruby and Rachel to hear firsthand how those challenges affect seniors, caregivers, and their families every day. Deb is committed to making sure New Mexicans can get the care they need to live with dignity and independence in their homes.
---
|
---
# **Consuelo's Place**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=22&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
The team at Consuelo’s Place is working hard to help people experiencing homelessness find stability and move into long-term housing. Deb was thrilled to learn more about their program. Their work shows what’s possible when housing is paired with the support people need to get back on their feet. As governor, Deb will tackle New Mexico’s housing crisis by building more affordable homes, protecting renters, and investing in behavioral health and substance use treatment that addresses the challenges that can lead to homelessness.
---
|
---
# **Rio Arriba Rally in the Valley**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=23&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
There are so many incredible candidates on the ballot this year. Deb joined Democratic candidates and supporters in Rio Arriba County for Rally in the Valley to celebrate the people stepping up to serve communities across New Mexico. Deb is ready to keep organizing, showing up, and working alongside Democrats across the state to make sure everyone has their voice heard by November 3rd.
---
|
---
# **Española Presbyterian Hospital Tour and Roundtable**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=24&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb toured Presbyterian Española Hospital and spoke with hospital leadership about the challenges facing rural healthcare and what it takes to keep quality care available close to home. When a rural hospital is struggling, patients can face longer drives, fewer providers, and delays in getting the care they need. As governor, Deb will work to address New Mexico’s doctor shortage, expand mobile health clinics, and strengthen the Health Care Affordability Fund so rural New Mexicans can get care when and where they need it.
---
|
---
# **Meet and Greets/Roadrunning Tour**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=25&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
Deb has continued to travel across New Mexico, meeting the people she hopes to serve as governor. From Clayton and Sapello to Carlsbad, Hobbs, Roswell, Clovis, Tucumcari, and every community in between, the final stretch of the Roadrunnin’ Tour gave her another chance to sit down with everyday New Mexicans, hear what’s on their minds, and learn what they want for the future of their communities. Meeting the people of New Mexico has always been Deb’s favorite part of this campaign, because this campaign has always been about them.
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17370?refcode=jtk1473-ot-nd&t=26&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
# **NewsNation**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17622?t=27&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
**“The Trump policies are making New Mexicans sicker, poorer, and hungrier. He’s cutting Medicaid, he’s slashing SNAP benefits.”**
---
Deb sat down with NewsNation to talk about her plans to lower costs and create more opportunities for New Mexico families, from protecting universal child care and strengthening educational opportunities for our kids to putting a pause on large-scale data center developments.
---
|
---
# **Source NM**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17624?t=28&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
**“Big tech’s mantra may be ‘move fast and break things,’ but here in New Mexico, we do things our way. The lack of transparency, the NDAs and backroom deals will never build trust with New Mexico communities.”**
---
This month, Deb announced she would enact an Executive Order on Day 1, putting a moratorium on new large-scale data center developments. Deb is committed to protecting New Mexico’s water, land, and people from Big Tech companies.
---
|
---
# **Santa Fe New Mexican**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17623?t=29&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
**“We need to inspire our high school students to go for careers in social work and behavioral health and other professions that we know we need here in the state, so I think those are all the kinds of places I would start.”**
---
This month, Deb announced that on Day One, she would sign an executive order placing a moratorium on new large-scale data center developments. Deb is committed to protecting New Mexico’s water, land, and communities and making sure Big Tech companies play by our rules, not the other way around.
---
|
---
# **KOAT**
---
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/17625?t=30&akid=13079%2E400544%2EYfbzt2)
---
**“Too often, corporations use new technology to maximize profits at the expense of our children’s safety and New Mexicans who work hard for a living, and our laws haven’t kept up to hold them accountable.”**
---
Deb joined Attorney General Torrez and Representative Serrato to support two proposed bills aimed at protecting children online and strengthening consumer protections. The legislation would establish a duty of care for social media, gaming, and consumer-facing AI companies whose products are designed for or marketed to children. Deb has pledged to support these protections as governor and hold tech companies accountable for keeping New Mexico kids safe online.
---

The State of Colorado has awarded more than $3 million in
sex-education grants to nearly two dozen school districts and charter
schools that adopted or planned to adopt the same human sexuality
education curriculum now at the center of a legal conflict between
parents and Roaring Fork School District — a curriculum that is free
to download.

Rights, Respect, Responsibility (3Rs) is a freely accessible K-12
comprehensive sexuality education curriculum created by activist
organization Advocates for Youth–a curriculum which some Colorado
parents have described as excessive, radical, and harmful. National
parental rights legal advocacy organization Alliance Defending Freedom
described the curriculum as “vulgar” in the legal notice it
delivered to RFSD on Aug. 11. In the letter, ADF accused the district
of violating parents’ rights, writing that parents have a
constitutional right “to know what their children are taught about
sex, gender, and their own bodies and to opt out when it conflicts
with their beliefs.”

body:
A generous supporter just made us an offer we can't pass up.
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter,
I have some BIG news, and I need your help to make the most of it.
A generous supporter has agreed to **match** up to $200,000 in donations for one specific purpose: putting billboards up across Texas before early voting starts.
**That means if we raise $200,000, we'll have $400,000 to put our message in front of millions of Texans on highways, in small towns, and in every corner of this state.** Every dollar you give today becomes two.
**Here's why this can't wait:** early voting in Texas starts on October 19. Around 70% of Texans will vote early or by mail, so for most voters, Election Day isn't November 3. It's just days away. Many will make up their minds in the next two weeks. If we want them to see our message before they cast their ballot, those billboards need to go up _now_.
Greg Abbott has twelve years and hundreds of millions of dollars to make sure Texans only hear his side of the story. This is our chance to reach voters who haven't heard ours yet, and to do it at **double the impact.**
**[Will you chip in now to help us hit our $200,000 billboard goal? Every dollar is matched until we hit it.](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20261008_2_match.vIz_sZ&refcode=em20261008-2364&t=1&akid=2364%2E299639%2E6Mn13h)**

On Monday night, at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Donald Trump was defending the rising costs of the war with Iran when he said, "They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego." He called it "a very small price to pay" and promised the war would be over "very soon." The White House _says_ he was making a different point entirely: that a nuclear-armed Iran would have been able to threaten American cities if it hadn't been stopped.
Read it however you like. This essay is not about that sentence. This essay is about **the midterms.**
But I'm opening with the remark because of **what tends to happen to remarks like it.** Notice how quickly the country moves past a sentence like that one. A president stands on a campaign stage, invokes Los Angeles and San Diego being "taken out," calls the cost of this war "a very small price to pay," and within a day we are arguing about something else. That is acclimatization, and it is one of the quietest and most reliable features of democratic decline. Things that would have dominated national life for months now survive for twelve hours, and we go to bed a little more tired and a little harder to shock.
So, in our apparently endless _what-the-actual-fuck_ timeline, let's talk about elections. The midterms are less than a month away.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/870efe8f-165c-4152-8662-426de342e2db?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

## Stop asking whether the election will be canceled
The question people keep reaching for is whether the election will happen at all. **Will it be canceled, postponed, swallowed by some emergency declaration?**
I understand the instinct. It's the version of the story we were raised on: the tanks, the silent radio, the constitution suspended on a Tuesday afternoon. It's also **the wrong model,** because it treats a coup as a single cinematic event.
The pattern political scientists have documented in country after country looks nothing like that. **You keep the ritual and you change the conditions.** You hold the election on schedule, with ballots and lines and a count, and you make sure that long before anyone votes, _the field has been tilted toward the people already in power._
Nic Cheeseman and Brian Klaas lay this out in their excellent book _[How to Rig an Election](https://substack.com/redirect/f6975862-3857-4dd1-a345-888d9c9140b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[.](https://substack.com/redirect/f6975862-3857-4dd1-a345-888d9c9140b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Their central finding is counterintuitive: electoral **autocrats frequently benefit from elections,** because a vote confers legitimacy at home and abroad and can actually _**extend**_ a regime's tenure rather than threaten it.
The toolbox they describe runs from patronage and bribery to coercion and information control, and, near the very bottom of the shelf, outright ballot fraud. Stuffing the box is usually the crudest method available. The most sophisticated operators rig the environment and leave the count alone.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.wC9GB7qui4IcfphxpQacprs9XsxstuBeivMo_cDO5lw?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=219469481)
## What "competitive authoritarianism" actually means
Whenever someone calls the United States authoritarian, somebody answers: _But we still have elections._
Exactly.
Modern authoritarianism does not require getting rid of elections. _**In many cases, elections are what make the system work.**_
Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way are not internet commentators tossing around a scary word. They originated the academic concept of competitive authoritarianism. In their framework, the formal machinery of democracy stays in place and the opposition really can win, but the people in power abuse the state so persistently that the contest is fundamentally unfair. Real competition, rigged terms.
In the October 2026 issue of the _Journal of Democracy_ , in an article titled ["Competitive Authoritarianism in America,"](https://substack.com/redirect/138c9881-1615-42c4-905e-46a533962b4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) they conclude that the United States has crossed that line during this second Trump term.
Elections remain real. But the Justice Department, the FBI and other agencies have been turned against critics, universities, law firms and the press, while national gerrymandering and coerced corporate money have skewed the competition. Scored against the eleven criteria they used to rate 35 regimes in their earlier work, the American case is comparable to Orban's Hungary, and far softer than 1990s Russia or Serbia.
They are not fatalists, and neither am I. They argue that this country's wealth, private sector and civil society dilute authoritarian abuse and make recovery through electoral turnover _possible_. They also warn that **turnover alone would not mean democracy came through intact.**
The game is tilted. It is not over.
[Leave me a one-time tip (thank you!)](https://substack.com/redirect/83e5cf8e-2c77-4f68-ae46-7502acafdbb9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
## The first tool: make losing look like cheating
The machinery starts working before a single ballot is cast. In 2020 the president lost, declared the election fraudulent, pressured state officials, and backed efforts to send alternate slates of electors to Congress. It all culminated on January 6th, and none of it was a one-time event. It is the precedent every later move leans on.
This year the same logic has a new setup. In February the president told NBC he would accept the midterm results "if the elections are honest," and that if they weren't, "something else has to happen." Days earlier, on a podcast, he said Republicans ought to "nationalize the voting" and take over elections in fifteen places. In that same NBC interview he named Detroit, Philadelphia and Atlanta as areas that are "unbelievably corrupt." He has promised to end mail-in ballots, which carried roughly three in ten votes cast in 2024, and in March he signed an executive order that would have imposed new federal requirements around mail voting and voter eligibility. Courts blocked major parts of it.
Watch what the _sequence_ does:
* It tells supporters that fraud is everywhere.
* It marks the opposition's strongholds as suspect by definition.
* It turns a loss into evidence of cheating.
* And it builds the permission structure for extraordinary action, because if the vote is dishonest, then "something else has to happen."

A normal politician asks what voters did. An authoritarian first asks whether the voters were _entitled to contradict him._

## The second tool: build the data
Since May 2025, the Justice Department has demanded voter-registration lists from state after state, including birthdates, driver's-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. Most states resisted, and the department sued dozens of them and the District of Columbia.
Meanwhile, voter records have been run through a citizenship lookup system housed at the Department of Homeland Security. In September, Reuters reported that DHS was reviewing voter-registration records from at least 47 states, and that hundreds of federal personnel had been assigned to an internal initiative to search those records for supposed noncitizen voters. In April, Common Cause sued to stop the creation of a national voter database and to keep voter data out of that screening program.
The lawsuits are only one part of the story, so **don 't get stuck on whether any particular lawsuit wins.** The more consequential asset may be _**the database itself.**_
A federal list of "questionable voters" does not have to identify enough illegal votes to overturn an election. It has to produce:
* a number big enough for a headline,
* a handful of frightening examples, and
* anomalies that can be presented as evidence that the result is contaminated.

That is what makes this infrastructure politically powerful: **it can manufacture doubt at national scale.**

## The third tool: turn voting-rights enforcement into election-crime enforcement
Context: the **Justice Department 's Civil Rights Division exists to protect people's access to the ballot.**
The Justice Department chapter of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation's blueprint for this administration, proposes shifting election-related prosecutions under Section 241 of Title 18 toward the Criminal Division. It complains that voter-registration fraud and improper ballot correction go uninvestigated.
**Within three months of the inauguration,** the Brennan Center documented the administration invoking that same statute in discussions of potential prosecutions involving election officials and voter-registration groups.
Project 2025 is legally sloppy about how the Justice Department currently divides these responsibilities. But the direction is unmistakable: **treat election administration as a crime scene.** Prioritize voter-registration fraud, ballot curing, and the people and organizations involved in helping people vote.
That **changes the posture of the institution.** Clerks, volunteers, registration groups and election workers stop being treated as the people who make democracy function and start being treated as potential suspects.

## The fourth tool: use the power of the state against the opposition
This one is not theoretical anymore. In September 2025 the president publicly told his Attorney General to act "NOW!!!" against James Comey, Letitia James and Sen. Adam Schiff. The U.S. attorney overseeing those cases had resisted, and he was pushed out. The president replaced him with his own former personal attorney, and indictments of Comey and James followed within weeks. Both cases were thrown out in November 2025 because the prosecutor had been unlawfully appointed, and a grand jury later declined to indict Letitia James again.
That is a plan that failed, and credit belongs to the judges and grand jurors who did their jobs. But look at what the attempt accomplished anyway, and what it teaches: the machinery of federal prosecution was pointed at people the president had publicly named as enemies.
Investigations involving Sen. Schiff and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook have been reported as well, and Levitsky and Way count the broader pattern, with the Justice Department, the FBI and other agencies turned on critics, universities, law firms and the press, among the defining features of the American case.
**Prosecution does not have to end in prison to work as political punishment.** Investigations drain money, produce headlines, frighten donors and lawyers, stigmatize organizations and shape the story the press tells. The process itself becomes the punishment, and then it becomes opposition campaign material.

## The fifth tool: put the federal government inside the machinery
Elections in this country are run by states and counties. The fifth tool is a steady push to put federal investigators, federal intelligence officials and federal rules inside that machinery.
On January 28, the FBI executed a search warrant at Fulton County's election hub in Georgia and carried out hundreds of boxes of ballots and records from 2020. The Director of National Intelligence at the time stood at the scene. The affidavit behind the search leaned on claims that had been debunked years earlier, and it traced the investigation to a White House appointee who had previously made unsupported claims about Arizona's voting system. The FBI has also obtained records from Arizona's post-2020 election investigations. Intelligence officials tested voting machines in Puerto Rico, and a cybersecurity contractor involved in that work reported finding no evidence of fraud. But the investigation did not simply stop there.
Then there is the Election Assistance Commission, the federal government's only independent commission devoted specifically to supporting election administration. Before its commissioners were removed, White House officials had reportedly spent months exploring ways to bypass the agency because it was not moving quickly enough on the voting-system and proof-of-citizenship changes the administration wanted. One proposal reportedly examined whether a national emergency over voting-system vulnerabilities could be used to force changes without the commission. That proposal was not implemented. Then, on July 9, four months before the midterms, the White House removed the commission's remaining members.
Notice the sequence: the administration wants changes, the independent commission does not move fast enough, officials explore ways around it, and then the commissioners are gone. The investigation goes looking for a vulnerability, the absence of evidence does not slow the expansion, and "security" becomes the reason federal authority has to grow.
This is how "election security" becomes a mechanism for accumulating election power:
* find a vulnerability,
* declare the existing safeguards inadequate, and
* use the danger as the argument for bringing more authority under executive control.

An **integrity crisis,** whether real or manufactured, is one of the oldest ways to pull power away from neutral, decentralized institutions and toward the executive.

## The sixth tool: weaken the referees, or change their job
Every contest needs referees, and the fastest way to tilt a game is to change who they answer to or take away their whistles.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency used to be the federal government's main partner to local election offices, helping them defend against hacks and physical threats. Project 2025 called for CISA to end its counter-disinformation work and confine its election assistance largely to basic cyber hygiene, and it also called for dismissing the agency's Cybersecurity Advisory Committee. Last year the administration cut roughly 1,000 CISA employees and slashed funding for two cybersecurity initiatives, one of them dedicated to election officials. Officials in some states describe their relationship with the agency this year as nonexistent, and several have paid for private services to fill the gap. CISA released its 2026 election-security plan on September 24, forty days before the election, and the administration's 2027 budget request would eliminate the program altogether.
Add the Election Assistance Commission, whose last members were removed in July. Add the Federal Election Commission, which regulates campaign finance rather than election administration (a different job, worth not confusing) and which lost its quorum in April 2025.
Different agencies. Different jobs. Same direction of travel: institutions designed to put distance between elections and presidential power are being weakened, emptied out, or pulled closer to the executive.
The question is not whether every change has the same purpose. The question is who still has the power to say **no** when the president wants something done to an election.

## The Grijalva precedent: the vote happened, and power sat on it
Adelita Grijalva won a special election in Arizona's 7th District on September 23, 2025. The result was never disputed. She was not sworn in for fifty days, a record, and for all of that time more than 800,000 people in southern Arizona had no voting member of the House. Her signature turned out to be the 218th on the discharge petition to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files, and she signed it shortly after she finally took the oath on November 12. The Speaker said the delay was about the government shutdown and the House schedule, not Epstein. Critics noted that Republicans who had won special elections were sworn in within days.
Forget the argument over motive for a moment and look at the precedent.
The voters made an undisputed choice. For seven weeks, one person with control of the doorway prevented that choice from taking effect.
That is the danger in miniature. Democracy depends not only on counting votes, but on powerful people accepting that a vote can bind them.
## Before we go abroad, notice the pattern
Here is why this can be hard to see while it is happening.
**Almost every piece comes with a respectable administrative explanation.**
Clean the voter rolls. Investigate fraud. Secure the machines. Prosecute crimes. Reform an agency. Delay a swearing-in.
You do not recognize the system by examining each lever in isolation. You recognize it by noticing that **the levers keep moving power in the same direction:** away from the opposition, away from independent institutions, and toward the people who will decide whether their own electoral defeats are legitimate.

## This has been done before
None of this requires a hypothetical. We have watched versions of this system develop, harden, fail and sometimes collapse all over the world.
Hungary is the closest comparison. For sixteen years Viktor Orban's government tilted the field with concentrated media, state resources, patronage and changes to election law. The rules were unfair, and the election was still competitive enough to lose. On April 12, turnout reached roughly 77 percent, the opposition Tisza party won a two-thirds parliamentary majority, and Orban conceded that night. That is the hopeful half of the entire literature in a single election: an unfair system can become deeply entrenched without becoming omnipotent.
Turkey shows a real opposition and genuinely consequential voting inside an unfair ecosystem. International observers in 2023 found that the incumbent enjoyed an unjustified advantage, with biased media coverage and restrictions on assembly and expression. Venezuela sits farther down the continuum. In 2024 the Carter Center concluded that the presidential election could not be considered democratic, pointing to restrictions on the opposition, a biased election authority and the failure to release results from individual polling stations.
Serbia is the story I'd hand to anyone who thinks the ending is written. Under Milošević there were elections, an opposition, and a regime that leaned on state media, patronage and repression. In 2000 the opposition beat him at the ballot box, and when his government tried to falsify the result, the public refused to accept it. Zimbabwe is the cautionary counterpart, with decades of elections held amid intimidation, patronage and selective violence. Russia shows the trajectory rather than the starting point: real competition after the Soviet collapse, then media capture, then legal constraints, then suppression of the opposition, until the elections continued but the uncertainty was gone. Competitive authoritarianism can harden into something worse.
Of course, America is not Venezuela. It is not Putin's Russia. But the point is, _**democracies do not become autocracies by waking up one morning already there.**_
The useful comparison is not between endpoints. It is between mechanisms -- and the mechanisms rhyme.

## The real genius of rigging: you never have to change a vote
**Election rigging does not require changing the vote count.** It means altering the conditions under which votes are cast, choices are offered, opposition is permitted to function, results are certified, and power is actually transferred.
Set the six tools beside the Grijalva case and the foreign examples, and one insight comes into focus: a sophisticated regime can win without touching a ballot. It decides who is allowed to vote and makes some ways of voting harder than others. It draws the maps. It dominates or frightens the press, harasses opposition organizations, and spends public resources as if they were campaign funds. It captures the referees, enforces the law selectively, and changes the rules late. It spreads enough fear and confusion that people stay home. It refuses to concede an adverse result, or delays carrying it out. Only when all of that has failed does crude ballot fraud become necessary.
This is the most useful lesson in Cheeseman and Klaas, and it is why "but the votes will be counted" is so unreassuring to me. Of course they will be cast, and they will be counted. The question is everything that happened before the counting, and everything that might happen after it.
## What to watch between now and November 3
Here is what I'll be watching, and what I'd ask you to watch too.
Before and during the voting, watch for new claims that particular Democratic cities are producing fraudulent registrations, and for federal officials announcing numbers of supposed noncitizen voters just before or during the count. Watch for warrants or subpoenas aimed at this year's machines, ballots or voter records, and for emergency declarations citing a cyberattack, foreign interference or machine vulnerabilities. Watch for attempts to move federal personnel into local election facilities, and for threats against the election workers who run them.
On election night and in the days after, watch for demands to stop counting late in the evening, and for ordinary ballot processing being described as "finding votes." Watch for lawsuits asking courts to discard whole categories of mail ballots after they have already been cast. Then watch the certification and the swearing-in: look for efforts to block certification in particular counties or states, and for delays in seating members who were duly elected.
And watch for the one shift that matters most. **It is the moment the message moves from "fraud might occur" to "we already know these results are fraudulent," before any evidence has been produced.** That is the escalation marker.
When you see it, you are no longer being asked to worry about an election. _You are being prepared to reject one._
## What democracy actually is
Democracy is not voting machines. It is not ballots, or campaign rallies, or the Capitol building. It is not even elections by themselves. **Democracy is a social and constitutional agreement:**_**people lend power to a government for a time, and the government gives it back when the people say so.**_
Every tool in this essay applies pressure on the second half of that sentence. And every example of that pressure being resisted, in Serbia, in Hungary, in a federal courtroom, in a grand jury room, **came from ordinary people who refused to treat power as something that belongs to whoever is holding it.** Voters, clerks, poll workers, judges, jurors.
The test of November isn't whether Americans are permitted to put pieces of paper into machines. The test is _whether those pieces of paper retain the power to remove the people currently governing us._
Authoritarians love elections when elections cannot cost them power.
Democracy begins **where they can.**

Notice how quickly the country moves past a sentence like that one. A president stands on a campaign stage, invokes Los Angeles and San Diego being "taken out," calls the cost of this war "a very small price to pay," and within a day we are arguing about something else. That is acclimatization, and it is one of the quietest and most reliable features of democratic decline. Things that would have dominated national life for months now survive for twelve hours, and we go to bed a little more tired and a little harder to shock. So, in our apparently endless what-the-actual-fuck timeline, let's talk about elections. Will it be canceled, postponed, swallowed by some emergency declaration? I understand the instinct. It's the version of the story we were raised on: the tanks, the silent radio, the constitution suspended on a Tuesday afternoon. It's also the wrong model, because it treats a coup as a single cinematic event. The pattern political scientists have documented in country after country looks nothing like that. You keep the ritual and you change the conditions. You hold the election on schedule, with ballots and lines and a count, and you make sure that long before anyone votes, the field has been tilted toward the people already in power. Nic Cheeseman and Brian Klaas lay this out in their excellent book Their central finding is counterintuitive: electoral autocrats frequently benefit from elections, because a vote confers legitimacy at home and abroad and can actually extend a regime's tenure rather than threaten it. The toolbox they describe runs from patronage and bribery to coercion and information control, and, near the very bottom of the shelf, outright ballot fraud. Stuffing the box is usually the crudest method available. The most sophisticated operators rig the environment and leave the count alone. What "competitive authoritarianism" actually means Whenever someone calls the United States authoritarian, somebody answers: But we still have elections. Exactly. Modern authoritarianism does not require getting rid of elections. In many cases, elections are what make the system work. Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way are not internet commentators tossing around a scary word. They originated the academic concept of competitive authoritarianism. In their framework, the formal machinery of democracy stays in place and the opposition really can win, but the people in power abuse the state so persistently that the contest is fundamentally unfair. Real competition, rigged terms. In the October 2026 issue of the Journal of Democracy , in an article titled they conclude that the United States has crossed that line during this second Trump term. Elections remain real. But the Justice Department, the FBI and other agencies have been turned against critics, universities, law firms and the press, while national gerrymandering and coerced corporate money have skewed the competition. Scored against the eleven criteria they used to rate 35 regimes in their earlier work, the American case is comparable to Orban's Hungary, and far softer than 1990s Russia or Serbia. They are not fatalists, and neither am I. They argue that this country's wealth, private sector and civil society dilute authoritarian abuse and make recovery through electoral turnover possible. They also warn that turnover alone would not mean democracy came through intact. The game is tilted. It is not over. The first tool: make losing look like cheating The machinery starts working before a single ballot is cast. In 2020 the president lost, declared the election fraudulent, pressured state officials, and backed efforts to send alternate slates of electors to Congress. In February the president told NBC he would accept the midterm results "if the elections are honest," and that if they weren't, "something else has to happen." Days earlier, on a podcast, he said Republicans ought to "nationalize the voting" and take over elections in fifteen places. In that same NBC interview he named Detroit, Philadelphia and Atlanta as areas that are "unbelievably corrupt." He has promised to end mail-in ballots, which carried roughly three in ten votes cast in 2024, and in March he signed an executive order that would have imposed new federal requirements around mail voting and voter eligibility. Courts blocked major parts of it. Watch what the sequence does: It tells supporters that fraud is everywhere. It marks the opposition's strongholds as suspect by definition. It turns a loss into evidence of cheating. And it builds the permission structure for extraordinary action, because if the vote is dishonest, then "something else has to happen." A normal politician asks what voters did. An authoritarian first asks whether the voters were entitled to contradict him. The second tool: build the data Since May 2025, the Justice Department has demanded voter-registration lists from state after state, including birthdates, driver's-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. Most states resisted, and the department sued dozens of them and the District of Columbia. Meanwhile, voter records have been run through a citizenship lookup system housed at the Department of Homeland Security. In September, Reuters reported that DHS was reviewing voter-registration records from at least 47 states, and that hundreds of federal personnel had been assigned to an internal initiative to search those records for supposed noncitizen voters. In April, Common Cause sued to stop the creation of a national voter database and to keep voter data out of that screening program. The lawsuits are only one part of the story, so don 't get stuck on whether any particular lawsuit wins. The more consequential asset may be the database itself. A federal list of "questionable voters" does not have to identify enough illegal votes to overturn an election. It has to produce: a number big enough for a headline, a handful of frightening examples, and anomalies that can be presented as evidence that the result is contaminated. That is what makes this infrastructure politically powerful: it can manufacture doubt at national scale. The third tool: turn voting-rights enforcement into election-crime enforcement Context: the Justice Department 's Civil Rights Division exists to protect people's access to the ballot. The Justice Department chapter of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation's blueprint for this administration, proposes shifting election-related prosecutions under Section 241 of Title 18 toward the Criminal Division. It complains that voter-registration fraud and improper ballot correction go uninvestigated. Within three months of the inauguration, the Brennan Center documented the administration invoking that same statute in discussions of potential prosecutions involving election officials and voter-registration groups. Project 2025 is legally sloppy about how the Justice Department currently divides these responsibilities. But the direction is unmistakable: treat election administration as a crime scene. Prioritize voter-registration fraud, ballot curing, and the people and organizations involved in helping people vote. That changes the posture of the institution. Clerks, volunteers, registration groups and election workers stop being treated as the people who make democracy function and start being treated as potential suspects. The fourth tool: use the power of the state against the opposition This one is not theoretical anymore. In September 2025 the president publicly told his Attorney General to act "NOW!!!" against James Comey, Letitia James and Sen. Adam Schiff. The U.S. attorney overseeing those cases had resisted, and he was pushed out. The president replaced him with his own former personal attorney, and indictments of Comey and James followed within weeks. Both cases were thrown out in November 2025 because the prosecutor had been unlawfully appointed, and a grand jury later declined to indict Letitia James again. That is a plan that failed, and credit belongs to the judges and grand jurors who did their jobs. But look at what the attempt accomplished anyway, and what it teaches: the machinery of federal prosecution was pointed at people the president had publicly named as enemies. Investigations involving Sen. Schiff and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook have been reported as well, and Levitsky and Way count the broader pattern, with the Justice Department, the FBI and other agencies turned on critics, universities, law firms and the press, among the defining features of the American case. Prosecution does not have to end in prison to work as political punishment. Investigations drain money, produce headlines, frighten donors and lawyers, stigmatize organizations and shape the story the press tells. The process itself becomes the punishment, and then it becomes opposition campaign material. The fifth tool: put the federal government inside the machinery Elections in this country are run by states and counties. The fifth tool is a steady push to put federal investigators, federal intelligence officials and federal rules inside that machinery. On January 28, the FBI executed a search warrant at Fulton County's election hub in Georgia and carried out hundreds of boxes of ballots and records from 2020. The Director of National Intelligence at the time stood at the scene. The affidavit behind the search leaned on claims that had been debunked years earlier, and it traced the investigation to a White House appointee who had previously made unsupported claims about Arizona's voting system. The FBI has also obtained records from Arizona's post-2020 election investigations. Intelligence officials tested voting machines in Puerto Rico, and a cybersecurity contractor involved in that work reported finding no evidence of fraud. But the investigation did not simply stop there. Then there is the Election Assistance Commission, the federal government's only independent commission devoted specifically to supporting election administration. Before its commissioners were removed, White House officials had reportedly spent months exploring ways to bypass the agency because it was not moving quickly enough on the voting-system and proof-of-citizenship changes the administration wanted. One proposal reportedly examined whether a national emergency over voting-system vulnerabilities could be used to force changes without the commission. That proposal was not implemented. Then, on July 9, four months before the midterms, the White House removed the commission's remaining members. Notice the sequence: the administration wants changes, the independent commission does not move fast enough, officials explore ways around it, and then the commissioners are gone. The investigation goes looking for a vulnerability, the absence of evidence does not slow the expansion, and "security" becomes the reason federal authority has to grow. This is how "election security" becomes a mechanism for accumulating election power: find a vulnerability, declare the existing safeguards inadequate, and use the danger as the argument for bringing more authority under executive control. An integrity crisis, whether real or manufactured, is one of the oldest ways to pull power away from neutral, decentralized institutions and toward the executive. The sixth tool: weaken the referees, or change their job Every contest needs referees, and the fastest way to tilt a game is to change who they answer to or take away their whistles. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency used to be the federal government's main partner to local election offices, helping them defend against hacks and physical threats. Project 2025 called for CISA to end its counter-disinformation work and confine its election assistance largely to basic cyber hygiene, and it also called for dismissing the agency's Cybersecurity Advisory Committee. Last year the administration cut roughly 1,000 CISA employees and slashed funding for two cybersecurity initiatives, one of them dedicated to election officials. Officials in some states describe their relationship with the agency this year as nonexistent, and several have paid for private services to fill the gap. CISA released its 2026 election-security plan on September 24, forty days before the election, and the administration's 2027 budget request would eliminate the program altogether. Add the Election Assistance Commission, whose last members were removed in July. Add the Federal Election Commission, which regulates campaign finance rather than election administration (a different job, worth not confusing) and which lost its quorum in April 2025. Different agencies. Different jobs. Same direction of travel: institutions designed to put distance between elections and presidential power are being weakened, emptied out, or pulled closer to the executive. The question is not whether every change has the same purpose. The question is who still has the power to say no when the president wants something done to an election. The Grijalva precedent: the vote happened, and power sat on it Adelita Grijalva won a special election in Arizona's 7th District on September 23, 2025. The result was never disputed. She was not sworn in for fifty days, a record, and for all of that time more than 800,000 people in southern Arizona had no voting member of the House. Her signature turned out to be the 218th on the discharge petition to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files, and she signed it shortly after she finally took the oath on November 12. The Speaker said the delay was about the government shutdown and the House schedule, not Epstein. Critics noted that Republicans who had won special elections were sworn in within days. Forget the argument over motive for a moment and look at the precedent. The voters made an undisputed choice. For seven weeks, one person with control of the doorway prevented that choice from taking effect. That is the danger in miniature. Democracy depends not only on counting votes, but on powerful people accepting that a vote can bind them. Before we go abroad, notice the pattern Here is why this can be hard to see while it is happening. Almost every piece comes with a respectable administrative explanation. Clean the voter rolls. Investigate fraud. Secure the machines. Prosecute crimes. Reform an agency. Delay a swearing-in. You do not recognize the system by examining each lever in isolation. You recognize it by noticing that the levers keep moving power in the same direction: away from the opposition, away from independent institutions, and toward the people who will decide whether their own electoral defeats are legitimate. This has been done before None of this requires a hypothetical. We have watched versions of this system develop, harden, fail and sometimes collapse all over the world. Hungary is the closest comparison. For sixteen years Viktor Orban's government tilted the field with concentrated media, state resources, patronage and changes to election law. The rules were unfair, and the election was still competitive enough to lose. On April 12, turnout reached roughly 77 percent, the opposition Tisza party won a two-thirds parliamentary majority, and Orban conceded that night. That is the hopeful half of the entire literature in a single election: an unfair system can become deeply entrenched without becoming omnipotent. Turkey shows a real opposition and genuinely consequential voting inside an unfair ecosystem. International observers in 2023 found that the incumbent enjoyed an unjustified advantage, with biased media coverage and restrictions on assembly and expression. Venezuela sits farther down the continuum. In 2024 the Carter Center concluded that the presidential election could not be considered democratic, pointing to restrictions on the opposition, a biased election authority and the failure to release results from individual polling stations. Serbia is the story I'd hand to anyone who thinks the ending is written. Under Milošević there were elections, an opposition, and a regime that leaned on state media, patronage and repression. In 2000 the opposition beat him at the ballot box, and when his government tried to falsify the result, the public refused to accept it. Zimbabwe is the cautionary counterpart, with decades of elections held amid intimidation, patronage and selective violence. Russia shows the trajectory rather than the starting point: real competition after the Soviet collapse, then media capture, then legal constraints, then suppression of the opposition, until the elections continued but the uncertainty was gone. Competitive authoritarianism can harden into something worse. Of course, America is not Venezuela. It is not Putin's Russia. But the point is, democracies do not become autocracies by waking up one morning already there. The useful comparison is not between endpoints. It is between mechanisms -- and the mechanisms rhyme. The real genius of rigging: you never have to change a vote Election rigging does not require changing the vote count. It means altering the conditions under which votes are cast, choices are offered, opposition is permitted to function, results are certified, and power is actually transferred. Set the six tools beside the Grijalva case and the foreign examples, and one insight comes into focus: a sophisticated regime can win without touching a ballot. It decides who is allowed to vote and makes some ways of voting harder than others. It draws the maps. It dominates or frightens the press, harasses opposition organizations, and spends public resources as if they were campaign funds. It captures the referees, enforces the law selectively, and changes the rules late. It spreads enough fear and confusion that people stay home. It refuses to concede an adverse result, or delays carrying it out. Only when all of that has failed does crude ballot fraud become necessary. This is the most useful lesson in Cheeseman and Klaas, and it is why "but the votes will be counted" is so unreassuring to me. Of course they will be cast, and they will be counted. The question is everything that happened before the counting, and everything that might happen after it. What to watch between now and November 3 Here is what I'll be watching, and what I'd ask you to watch too. Before and during the voting, watch for new claims that particular Democratic cities are producing fraudulent registrations, and for federal officials announcing numbers of supposed noncitizen voters just before or during the count. Watch for warrants or subpoenas aimed at this year's machines, ballots or voter records, and for emergency declarations citing a cyberattack, foreign interference or machine vulnerabilities. Watch for attempts to move federal personnel into local election facilities, and for threats against the election workers who run them. On election night and in the days after, watch for demands to stop counting late in the evening, and for ordinary ballot processing being described as "finding votes." Watch for lawsuits asking courts to discard whole categories of mail ballots after they have already been cast. Then watch the certification and the swearing-in: look for efforts to block certification in particular counties or states, and for delays in seating members who were duly elected. And watch for the one shift that matters most. It is the moment the message moves from "fraud might occur" to "we already know these results are fraudulent," before any evidence has been produced. That is the escalation marker. When you see it, you are no longer being asked to worry about an election. You are being prepared to reject one. What democracy actually is Democracy is not voting machines. It is not ballots, or campaign rallies, or the Capitol building. It is not even elections by themselves. Democracy is a social and constitutional agreement:people lend power to a government for a time, and the government gives it back when the people say so. Every tool in this essay applies pressure on the second half of that sentence. And every example of that pressure being resisted, in Serbia, in Hungary, in a federal courtroom, in a grand jury room, came from ordinary people who refused to treat power as something that belongs to whoever is holding it. Voters, clerks, poll workers, judges, jurors. The test of November isn't whether Americans are permitted to put pieces of paper into machines. The test is whether those pieces of paper retain the power to remove the people currently governing us. Authoritarians love elections when elections cannot cost them power. Democracy begins where they can. Sources / Further Reading Cheeseman, Nic, and Brian Klaas. How to Rig an Election. Revised and expanded edition. Yale University Press, 2024. name: Denise Bianco
subject: Help Me Wish Sheriff Bianco a Happy Birthday! 🎂
body:
A Special Birthday Message from His Wife, Denise Bianco

| | | | | |
---
| |

Dear Friend,
This is Denise Bianco, proud wife of Sheriff Chad Bianco. **Today is a very special day for our family. It's Chad's birthday!**
I've had the blessing of standing by Chad's side as his wife, watching him dedicate his life to protecting others. Through the long nights, missed family moments, and sacrifices that come with wearing the badge, I've seen firsthand the love he has for our community.
For **33 years** , Chad has devoted his life to protecting our children, our seniors, and our families.
But beyond the badge, I know Chad as a **loving husband, devoted father, proud grandfather, and man of faith.** I couldn't be prouder of the man I married.
**Today, I have one special request.**
---
| [Wish Chad a happy birthday!](https://us.list-manage.com/zsjlomXSpMY?e=1facf02470&c2id=205919520b3860dafbe9b9f5dda2019d)
---
| | | | | |
Will you join me in wishing my husband and your Sheriff a happy birthday?

Chad has spent his life fighting for us. **Now, it's our turn to fight for him.** We're all going to need to stand behind our warrior in 2028. Please consider making a contribution to his Sheriff 2028 re-election campaign and help us keep Chad fighting for Riverside County.
With love and gratitude,
**Denise Bianco** Proud Wife of Sheriff Chad Bianco
---

Gov. Janet Mills has joined four other Democratic governors who insist their states can't ask Medicaid welfare recipients to work -- or look for work -- in exchange for taxpayer-funded benefits.
In an Oct. 1 letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Mills and her counterparts asked the Trump administration to delay the Jan. 1, 2027, compliance deadline. They proposed no replacement date.
The Mills Administration has known since at least July 4, 2025, when President Donald Trump signed the work requirements into law, that Medicaid welfare, known in Maine as MaineCare, would require new, tighter limits. The federal government published guidance for state agencies in Dec. 2025.
The move is just the latest step by Maine Democrats to resist policies that would encourage work over dependence on welfare programs.
Subscribe to The Robinson Report for updates on how Augusta spends your paycheck for you!
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..ZFOF40nKFt66PjzxbVeQFcG3EVxguOZZvxTXJ6xBICA?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=219467617)
In 2018, former Republican Gov. Paul LePage had obtained federal permission to impose work requirements on Maine's costliest welfare program.
However, Mills [rejected](https://substack.com/redirect/b18d48bd-48d7-44e9-bd5b-78f6a7f0bf02?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the opportunity in 2019 while simultaneously expanding the welfare program to able-bodied childless adults. Later, Mills worked with Democratic lawmakers, including then-Senate President Troy Jackson, to expand access to the welfare program to a broader class of non-citizens.
The [federal rule](https://substack.com/redirect/b2192cac-bcef-4de3-ac9f-cec52f128dda?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) generally applies to Medicaid expansion adults ages 19 through 64. Recipients can satisfy it through 80 hours of qualifying work, community service or other approved activities in a month, half-time school enrollment, or qualifying earnings. Exemptions cover pregnant women, certain caregivers, people with disabilities or medical frailty, and other specified groups.
"We have been candid from the outset that we oppose these requirements as a matter of policy," the governors wrote.
The plea for a delay comes as the same welfare bureaucracy in Maine struggles to police fraudulent welfare providers and answer congressional questions about spending on noncitizens.
Even as Mills has publicly characterized allegations of widespread welfare fraud and abuse as political attacks, her Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) suspended payments to providers investigated by The Maine Wire, terminated four autism care agencies accused of neglecting disabled adults, and froze applications from new providers in four MaineCare programs. Federal investigators, meanwhile, have demanded answers about tens of millions of dollars in improper payments under child autism programs. Separately, the House Oversight Committee is investigating whether DHHS illegally caused the federal government to pay for welfare benefits provided to noncitizens.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger also signed the letter. The five governors contend that a June 1 federal rule departed from earlier guidance and left states insufficient time to revise eligibility systems, train employees and notify recipients.
"These are not minor or technical adjustments," they wrote. "They fundamentally change the processes and system logic underlying states' implementation plans."
The Democrats have asked Kennedy to use federal enforcement discretion to delay compliance until state systems are ready. Although the letter says, "We are not requesting an indefinite postponement," its proposed substitute for a deadline is "demonstrated readiness." It supplies neither a new date nor individual schedules for the five states.
Mills' own department is already [telling MaineCare recipients](https://substack.com/redirect/3dbc0ee1-0b26-4d76-8415-efda4dc279db?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the requirements begin Jan. 1. Its guidance lists monthly earnings of at least $580 as one way to comply and says affected members will receive notices ahead of their 2027 renewals.
The affected population exists because of the expansion Mills made her first priority as governor.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..ZFOF40nKFt66PjzxbVeQFcG3EVxguOZZvxTXJ6xBICA?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=219467617)
Her first executive order in January 2019 directed implementation of the Medicaid expansion voters approved in 2017 and Gov. LePage had successfully resisted. By September 2019, more than 37,000 people had enrolled, and adults without children accounted for 81% of the expansion population, [the Maine Wire reported](https://substack.com/redirect/fa137ec2-b48f-403f-a3e9-d40f6b35c9bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). The state's two-year budget included $125 million for expansion. As of the most recent update from the state, 72,623 childless, able-bodied adults are enrolled in the welfare program, while total enrollment is roughly 380,000.
In resisting expansion of MaineCare, LePage predicted that adding able-bodied childless adults to Maine's largest welfare program would destroy the state's budget and prompt financial crises. LePage's warnings look prophetic now that the state faces a $1.3 billion forecasted shortfall for the next biennial budget -- a deficit that was preceded by an "unexpected" 2025 shortfall of $118 million, which Democrats used as an opportunity to raise taxes. In both cases, the overspending was driven by the runaway costs of the Medicaid welfare program.
Troy Jackson, then Senate president and now the Democratic nominee challenging Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, [supported expanding MaineCare to able-bodied, childless adults and noncitizens](https://substack.com/redirect/985388db-43c2-49ba-88a9-45bfeeda42d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Under Mills and the Democratic Legislature, coverage widened again: Beginning in July 2022, [noncitizen](https://substack.com/redirect/7cb83ad1-6b7a-4cda-bcb0-55bb57f02c18?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) children and pregnant women could qualify for MaineCare or related children's coverage regardless of immigration status.
A federal inspector general's audit estimated at least $45.6 million in improper MaineCare payments for children's autism services in 2023, including $28.7 million in federal funds. Every one of the 100 sampled enrollee-months contained errors. Auditors identified missing [assessments](https://substack.com/redirect/23fe2f9f-4ab7-412f-83fd-6caa49a7fe23?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), inadequate billing documentation, copied treatment notes and charges involving nontherapy time.
That audit prompted Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz to demand records and answers in February. Maine asked for another 30 days. Oz refused.
"After careful consideration, CMS is unable to grant the requested extension," Oz wrote in the letter [obtained by The Robinson Report](https://substack.com/redirect/948e84c9-5975-437c-91ba-f527afe85416?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Mills responded by rejecting allegations of widespread fraud, attacking the investigation's motives and defending her administration's enforcement record. In her [March 6 response](https://substack.com/redirect/799ef52f-bf95-43c7-9fe4-ab8b0d31da53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), she argued that federal officials had predetermined the outcome and were using fraud allegations for political purposes.
DHHS suspended Gateway Community Services LLC's payments Dec. 23, 2025, after finding a "credible allegation of fraud." Audits spanning several years identified roughly $1.7 million in questioned reimbursements. Gateway denied intentionally defrauding MaineCare, attributing the disputes to documentation and billing issues, but [did not appeal the continued suspension](https://substack.com/redirect/f2cf0f3d-1b94-4581-9744-09cf58221795?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) by its July deadline.
Another case followed Maine Wire reporting by eight days.
DHHS suspended Maine Connect Care's payments Jan. 30 after The Maine Wire visited its Portland office and published a report on the business. The suspension notice alleged billing for services never provided, services delivered while unlicensed, and services involving an excluded individual. The company billed MaineCare more than $7.2 million from 2021 through 2025, according to [records obtained through the Freedom of Access Act](https://substack.com/redirect/1c2ac22e-a775-423d-8a11-ff4433fb24d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). The notice did not identify which source of information triggered the investigation.
At Paradise Residential Services, the failures extended to the treatment of disabled Mainers.
A March termination letter cited inadequate food, unsanitary homes, failures in employee screening and medication management, and residents "repeatedly left without staff." The state's records documented problems dating to 2024, yet DHHS countersigned a new provider agreement in November 2025. Inspections the following month produced findings of immediate jeopardy, [the Maine Wire reported after obtaining the records](https://substack.com/redirect/a2b458c0-7aaf-485e-a0fe-1ea2dd7af62e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
By April, the administration was restricting entry into entire programs.
Effective April 13, DHHS [paused initial provider applications](https://substack.com/redirect/d3cbd4e2-c2f6-4724-b326-304775d7e126?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) for MaineCare Sections 18, 20, 21 and 29, which serve adults with brain injuries, intellectual disabilities, autism and related conditions. The department cited application volume, limited staff and the need to oversee existing providers.
Later that month, it delayed certain pharmacy payments until the new fiscal year because additional funding would not be available before July 1, [The Robinson Report disclosed](https://substack.com/redirect/1234c0be-a082-4c55-aa7d-28dd3cbe5a84?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2246936&post_id=219467617&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjE5NDY3NjE3LCJpYXQiOjE3OTE0ODY5NjksImV4cCI6MTc5NDA3ODk2OSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTIyNDY5MzYiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.YBTlIF3ybXIiPy5MDecZx_iXwCwL-qsSe8Mo2F9KL5E)
The administration's handling of Congress' Medicaid investigation offers another example of its approach to federal oversight.
[Emails obtained by The Robinson Report under the Freedom of Access Act](https://substack.com/redirect/f77ee822-ea51-4fb0-bb68-ce17ab493f78?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) showed DHHS coordinating its response with other Democratic-led states, including Colorado, Minnesota, New York, California, Illinois and Oregon, while the governor's office supervised what Maine would disclose.
On Sept. 19, 2025, Commissioner Sara Gagne-Holmes told officials to keep the governor's office involved and "check in with them before we produce any data."
"The goal here is to avoid a congressional subpoena," she wrote.
House Oversight Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., had sought records about Medicaid spending on people without lawful immigration status and whether states improperly charged Washington for their care. Maine limited its production to emergency-only coverage and reported $14.6 million in payments from 2019 through July 2025. That accounting excluded noncitizen benefits covered via MaineCare's General Fund expenditures.
The emails document a deliberate effort to control the disclosure. They do not, by themselves, establish that the excluded spending was unlawful.
As for the work requirement, Maine's employment figures offer Mills little basis for arguing that jobs are unavailable.
The governor has [touted low unemployment as evidence of her economic record](https://substack.com/redirect/2d88b308-dadb-4a36-aba1-33b3b1e9c4ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Maine's unemployment rate was 3.1% in July, roughly a percentage point below the national rate, according to [state labor figures](https://substack.com/redirect/6d0f6384-1edf-442b-b1b0-3a37c6d0abce?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Historically, high unemployment has provided a rationale for waiving welfare work rules, particularly in the food stamp program. [The Maine Wire covered that dispute in 2023](https://substack.com/redirect/e7015cd5-7312-44aa-88df-11eba74203d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), when Republicans urged Mills not to seek another waiver while employers were looking for workers.
The new Medicaid rule also allows temporary hardship exceptions in counties with sufficiently high unemployment. That is different from the statewide implementation delay Mills now seeks.
If Mills' account of Maine's job market is correct, a shortage of jobs supplies no statewide justification for postponement. The letter instead asks Washington to accept that, after months of preparation, her administration needs more time to make its systems work.
The governors' letter offers no Maine-specific estimate of what postponing work requirements would cost, no schedule for completing Maine's eligibility systems and no date by which Mills says her department will be ready.
"We ask that you delay the January 1, 2027 compliance date until states can implement the law as the IFR now requires," the governors wrote.
For now, Maine's own guidance still tells recipients to prepare for Jan. 1.

Dear Friend, this is your only warning. What I'm about to share with you is emotional \- PREPARE YOURSELF. ** The Rose Garden is almost sacred at night. When the cameras are gone and the noise of the day finally fades, it stops being a backdrop for press conferences and power plays. It becomes what it was always meant to be: a quiet, living garden right beside the White House. And last evening, in what could be my final 4 weeks as President, I took some time to reflect on the last 10 years we have shared as I strolled alongside the rose bushes. ****** Your faith in me still humbles me more than I can put into words. From the highest of highs to the lowest of lows, I have always been able to count on your support. From an unproven, underdog political candidate to the leader of our nation's GREATEST movement in history, you have always stood by my side. Even when it would have been easier to write me off. For the past decade, the Radical Left has done everything in their power in an attempt to destroy the MAGA coalition. They came for me, my family, friends, and above all: my supporters. People like you, Friend. When the chips were down, you stared evil straight in the face and never flinched. You put your career, family, and even LIFE on the line to continue supporting me, and I will never be able to thank you enough. Every single day I wake up, I pray and thank God for his blessing of being able to be your President. And every night I go to sleep, I pray for the opportunity to spend one more day fighting to make America Great Again. And in the Rose Garden late last evening, I made one final prayer before leaving: That my supporters will keep their trust in me one final time and help see the rest of my mission through. As you read my message, the Radical Left all across the country are rallying. From our cities to the countryside, dangerous socialists and communists are preparing to destroy our Republican Majorities in the House and the Senate. I refuse to go quietly and allow the Radical Left one final victory. After everything we have built - after the strength we restored, the borders we secured, the voices we gave back to forgotten Americans - we cannot stop when we are so close to Making America Great Again. body:
Are you ready to help flip the House?

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/30f1734f066e/join-me-rep-diana-degette-for-lunch-in-ca-17667020?e=feea60f246)
