| |

### Dear Peter,

For the last two years, Donald Trump has driven a political agenda defined by division. He’s sought to divide our communities, our party, our values, and even innocent families. All so he and his billionaire friends can get even richer.

While Trump may not be on the ballot in 2026, his dangerous actions, vile rhetoric, and disastrous policies ARE on the ballot. This November, Democrats have an opportunity to vote out MAGA extremists in Congress and take back the House.
---
| [CLICK HERE TO JOIN ME](https://us.list-manage.com/wEaJk4yAawt?e=feea60f246&c2id=eff6f64158732e8851993770f57c9616)
---
| |
But to do so, our party must be united in our opposition against authoritarianism. That unity starts right here in our community.
**That’s why I’m hosting my annual Fall Luncheon on Thursday October 22nd in Daly City from 12pm-1:30pm.** Will you join me?
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/UvW_AWa5dbm?e=feea60f246&c2id=eff6f64158732e8851993770f57c9616)
| |
Unified party opposition is critical. But we must also find unity in how we rebuild after taking back majorities. My House Democratic colleagues and I have real plans for how to materially impact people’s lives on day one. We will work to create an economy that works for everyone, undo Trump’s damage to our climate, and establish a brighter future for the next generation.
---
| [CLICK HERE TO JOIN ME ](https://us.list-manage.com/iMVI9u6o70j?e=feea60f246&c2id=eff6f64158732e8851993770f57c9616)
---
| |
I hope to see you at my upcoming Fall Luncheon. I’ll share some stories from the campaign trail, updates from D.C., and discuss how our party can forge a new path after the Midterms to carry the Blue Wave into 2028. **Click below to RSVP.**

For more info contact Carol Ong at [ong102825@aol.com](mailto:ong102825@aol.com).

| | | Eight years ago, I became the first openly gay person elected to the Michigan State Senate.
---
The Senate was talking about us. It was making decisions for us. But it wasn't actually listening to us.
If you're not at the table, oftentimes you find yourself on the menu.
I ran and won, and brought our voice into the rooms where decisions about us are being made.
**Now I'm running for Congress in Michigan's 11th District, and if we win in November, I'll be the first openly gay member of Congress in Michigan history.**
That barrier has stood for as long as Michigan has sent people to Washington. It doesn't break on its own. It breaks because people decide to do the work, election after election.
In 2023, I stood on the floor of the Michigan Senate and led the fight to pass a bill that Republicans had blocked for decades. I sponsored the amendment to Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, adding sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes from discrimination.
That same term, I helped pass a ban on conversion therapy for minors in Michigan, strengthen Michigan's hate crime law, and make it easier for trans Michiganders to obtain government documents that match their identity.

clean_body: | | | | = | | | Eight years ago, I became the first openly gay person elected to the Michigan State Senate. The Senate was talking about us. It was making decisions for us. But it wasn't actually listening to us. If you're not at the table, oftentimes you find yourself on the menu. I ran and won, and brought our voice into the rooms where decisions about us are being made. Now I'm running for Congress in Michigan's 11th District, and if we win in November, I'll be the first openly gay member of Congress in Michigan history. That barrier has stood for as long as Michigan has sent people to Washington. It doesn't break on its own. It breaks because people decide to do the work, election after election. In 2023, I stood on the floor of the Michigan Senate and led the fight to pass a bill that Republicans had blocked for decades. I sponsored the amendment to Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, adding sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes from discrimination. That same term, I helped pass a ban on conversion therapy for minors in Michigan, strengthen Michigan's hate crime law, and make it easier for trans Michiganders to obtain government documents that match their identity. = | | | | | = | | | = | | | = | | | = | | | | = | | Thank you, Jeremy | | | | | | = | | | | | | Paid for by Jeremy Moss for Congress | | Jeremy Moss for Congress 2211 S Telegraph Rd PO Box 7023 Bloomfield Hills, MI 48302 United States | | | | | | | | | | = | | | = | | This message was sent to dpwillis67@gmail.com. | |

| | | Picture your ballot showing up by certified mail. If you're not home to sign for it, it goes back. According to new reporting from ProPublica, **that's how the Trump White House first wanted mail voting to work.**
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/140980396/652138843/-569431239?refcode=261008-mail&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDcvMS83NzI2MCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI1YzEzNWNjZi01MGMzLWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E0ZmJlODMiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=KZEfLgDroa0OZpcgfOiuLQfL7tnnrSjpjd1omLiRMsw=)
---
The administration floated a plan to require every ballot to be delivered by certified mail. It was dropped only after the Postal Service warned that it would be impossible to carry out. The plan they ended up with was hardly better. Trump's March executive order would have turned postal workers into gatekeepers, deciding which ballots got delivered and which didn't. It put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has no formal authority over the Postal Service, in charge of coordinating it. Postal officials were left out of key conversations, and the order's contents shocked even the Postal Service's own lawyers. **Then the White House insisted that if even one envelope in a batch didn't match a state's voter list, the whole batch should be rejected.** A former postal official told ProPublica what that would mean: **_"If four addresses don't align in a mailing of one million, 999,996 other people don't get their ballot tomorrow."_** Oregon votes entirely by mail. In our state, that would not cause a “glitch” – it would have resulted in our election grinding to a halt. The Supreme Court blocked the order last month. But the reporting makes one thing clear: this was never just a careless mistake. It took nearly a year of planning by people who knew exactly how much disruption they were designing. **They won't stop at one order. As your Secretary of State, I'm going to keep Oregon's vote-by-mail system working for every eligible voter, no matter what the Trump Administration tries next. To do that, I need people standing with me before the next attack comes.** **[Can you chip in $15 to my campaign right now and help us stand up to Trump's attacks on vote-by-mail? ](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/140980399/652138846/-569431239?refcode=261008-mail&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDcvMS83NzI2MCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI1YzEzNWNjZi01MGMzLWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDBkM2E0ZmJlODMiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=KZEfLgDroa0OZpcgfOiuLQfL7tnnrSjpjd1omLiRMsw=)**

| | Welcome back to Fact Friday — a day early this week. **Today is Latina Equal Pay Day, a day that shines a light on one of the widest wage gaps in our country. And the date itself tells part of the story.** Latina Equal Pay Day marks how far into the year Latinas would have to work to catch up to what white, non-Hispanic men earned the year before. Today, Latinas earn about **53 cents for every dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men** when all workers are counted. Even among full-time, year-round workers, Latinas earn only about 60 cents on the dollar. Over the course of a 40-year career, that gap adds up to roughly**$1.2 million in lost earnings.** And here in Texas, the gap can be even greater: Latinas stand to lose about **$1.7 million over the course of their careers.** That means less money to pay rent or a mortgage, put food on the table, care for family, save for retirement, start a business, or build wealth to pass down to the next generation. **Here in El Paso, where Latinas power so much of our workforce and our community, equal pay is an economic issue that affects**** _all of us_****.** Closing the gap means making sure workers are paid fairly for their work, strengthening workplace protections, expanding access to good-paying jobs, and ensuring every family has a fair shot at economic security. Latinas should not have to work**nearly ten months longer** just to earn what someone else earned the year prior. **That is why I will keep fighting for an economy where equal work means equal pay — and where every worker has the opportunity to build a secure future.** If you learned something from today's Fact Friday, share this email with someone who should know what Latina Equal Pay Day really means. Staying informed is power. Let's use it, El Paso. And here in Texas, the gap can be even greater: Latinas stand to lose about $1.7 million over the course of their careers. That means less money to pay rent or a mortgage, put food on the table, care for family, save for retirement, start a business, or build wealth to pass down to the next generation. Here in El Paso, where Latinas power so much of our workforce and our community, equal pay is an economic issue that affects all of us. Closing the gap means making sure workers are paid fairly for their work, strengthening workplace protections, expanding access to good-paying jobs, and ensuring every family has a fair shot at economic security. Latinas should not have to worknearly ten months longer just to earn what someone else earned the year prior. That is why I will keep fighting for an economy where equal work means equal pay — and where every worker has the opportunity to build a secure future. If you learned something from today's Fact Friday, share this email with someone who should know what Latina Equal Pay Day really means. Staying informed is power. Let's use it, El Paso. Nearly 12,000 book bans in one school year. When a number like that lands, the mind reaches for a supply chain: publishers must be pumping out thousands of objectionable titles a year to stock this much shelvable trouble. That's the question worth asking -- so I asked it, and ran the math. The answer is the part nobody on either side wants printed: roughly none. The supply was never the variable. The enforcement was.
Start with the ledger from PEN America's new report, released Monday during Banned Books Week. In the 2025-26 school year, public schools logged 11,982 removals affecting 7,370 unique titles -- the work of some 4,000 authors -- up 74% from 6,870 the year before, and the highest total since PEN began tracking in 2021. More than 22,800 bans have accumulated across 45 states in five years. But the geography is the tell: Texas recorded over 8,100 bans and Florida over 3,200 -- roughly 94% of the national total in two states. Texas took the top spot for the first time because of SB 13, which lets districts purge books by broad category rather than case by case. If publishers' output were driving this, the bans would track publishing markets -- New York, L.A., wherever books are made. Instead they track statutes.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/40b68910-0f34-47fe-93f5-bab1c47da60c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Now the supply side. Roughly four million new titles appear in American ISBN databases each year, which sounds alarming until you see what that actually is: mostly self-published print-on-demand slush, AI-generated filler, and reprints that will never come within a mile of a school library. Traditional publishing's frontlist is a fraction of that. And the segment that ban rhetoric is actually aimed at -- children's and young adult books -- is measured in thousands. The Cooperative Children's Book Center received 3,619 U.S. children's and YA books in 2024; about 7% -- call it 250 titles -- had LGBTQ themes or characters. That is the entire annual national output of the most-challenged genre category on the most-scrutinized theme. Ban every single one the day it publishes and you haven't filled a tenth of this year's ban count. To hit 4,500 newly flagged titles from new supply alone, you'd have to condemn essentially the whole yearly catalogue of young-adult literature, plus change.
And the flagged list isn't new books. This year's haul includes Jane Eyre (1847). It includes The Shining (1977) -- Stephen King, pulled 312 times, was the most-banned author in America for the second straight year, an author whose work has sat on school shelves longer than most school boards have existed. The Handmaid's Tale (1985). Speak (1999). Crank (2004). Sold (2006) -- a twenty-year-old National Book Award finalist about child trafficking, and the single most-banned title. Add Tokyo Ghoul manga and you have the full picture: this is backlist. This is the accumulated inventory of American letters, being swept off shelves not because it arrived last Tuesday but because someone finally decided to conduct an inventory review.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/169b62cb-e56c-487b-b251-0a959047c91a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
What actually grew between the quiet 2010s and now is the machinery of removal. State laws that purge by category. Directives that require pulling a book first and reviewing it later. Mass challenges driven by circulating watchlists. And this year's newest tool, confirmed in public records the Texas Freedom to Read Project shared with PEN: school administrators consulting AI chatbots, which recommended removing books -- not because they met any legal standard of obscenity, but, in documented cases, because another district had removed them. Sit with that. A machine in one county clearing a shelf because a machine in another county cleared a shelf. A keyword scanner cannot read Speak and understand it is a novel about the aftermath of rape that a survivor needs to find; it can only see the word. It cannot see that Sold is an argument against the thing it depicts. PEN's Philomena Polefrone put the operating condition plainly: "Confusing and vague state book ban laws and chilling directives from state politicians have created chaos and fear." The AI didn't create the chaos. It industrialized it.
To be fair to the supply-side intuition: the catalogue did shift after 2020 -- the CCBC found 51% of children's books it received in 2024 had significant BIPOC content -- and some genuinely explicit material did land in school libraries in that period, to parents' entirely legitimate objection. Curation is not censorship; no student is owed any particular title. And PEN's counting is generous -- a book pulled for a week counts the same as one pulped, which is why the American Library Association's stricter, permanent-removal-only ledger says 5,600. Halve PEN's number. Quarter it. The arithmetic still doesn't reach publishing output, because the books on the shelves haven't changed much in a generation. What changed is what's being done to the shelves.
**Does it matter?**
Reading scores are the worst since the test began -- twelfth graders reading at levels not seen in the entire history of the exam, roughly a third of eighth graders below "basic," which is the polite federal word for *can't do it* -- and the newest national mood is a shrug: does it really matter anyway? It matters, but not the way the press releases say. Not primarily because the economy needs workers, though it does. It matters because reading is the only technology we have for thinking a thought that isn't being streamed to us. A kid who can't read isn't just locked out of Faulkner; he's locked out of the fine print -- the lease, the loan, the ballot measure, the label on the prescription bottle -- which means somebody else will always be happy to explain the world to him, briefly, persuasively, and for a fee. A republic of non-readers becomes a republic of listeners, and listeners get governed by whoever has the loudest feed. The decline took thirty years to register in the data; the consequence doesn't show up in the data at all. It shows up later, in the voting booth and the jury box, when a citizen who was never taught to read deeply has to decide whom to believe -- and picks the confident voice over the true one. So yes. It matters. It's the only score that ever mattered.

Here is the number that ends the argument: 11,982 bans divided by 7,370 books is 1.6 bans per book. The same titles are being removed, district after district, in bulk, by list, by category, by chatbot. That is not a community reacting to what its libraries contain. That is a process propagating itself. The objectionable-book pipeline the question assumes doesn't exist -- publishers never built anything close to it. You don't need twelve thousand objectionable books a year to get twelve thousand bans. You just need vague laws, circulating lists, and a machine that clears a shelf without ever reading a page -- and someone in the statehouse willing to call that a review.
The books weren't the problem. The objections were manufactured at home.

clean_body: 12,000 book bans in one school year. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? 12,000 book bans in one school year. | | | Oct 8 | | | | | | | | | | | | Nearly 12,000 book bans in one school year. When a number like that lands, the mind reaches for a supply chain: publishers must be pumping out thousands of objectionable titles a year to stock this much shelvable trouble. That's the question worth asking -- so I asked it, and ran the math. The answer is the part nobody on either side wants printed: roughly none. The supply was never the variable. The enforcement was. Start with the ledger from PEN America's new report, released Monday during Banned Books Week. In the 2025-26 school year, public schools logged 11,982 removals affecting 7,370 unique titles -- the work of some 4,000 authors -- up 74% from 6,870 the year before, and the highest total since PEN began tracking in 2021. More than 22,800 bans have accumulated across 45 states in five years. But the geography is the tell: Texas recorded over 8,100 bans and Florida over 3,200 -- roughly 94% of the national total in two states. Texas took the top spot for the first time because of SB 13, which lets districts purge books by broad category rather than case by case. If publishers' output were driving this, the bans would track publishing markets -- New York, L.A., wherever books are made. Instead they track statutes. | | ---|---|--- Now the supply side. Roughly four million new titles appear in American ISBN databases each year, which sounds alarming until you see what that actually is: mostly self-published print-on-demand slush, AI-generated filler, and reprints that will never come within a mile of a school library. Traditional publishing's frontlist is a fraction of that. And the segment that ban rhetoric is actually aimed at -- children's and young adult books -- is measured in thousands. The Cooperative Children's Book Center received 3,619 U.S. children's and YA books in 2024; about 7% -- call it 250 titles -- had LGBTQ themes or characters. That is the entire annual national output of the most-challenged genre category on the most-scrutinized theme. Ban every single one the day it publishes and you haven't filled a tenth of this year's ban count. To hit 4,500 newly flagged titles from new supply alone, you'd have to condemn essentially the whole yearly catalogue of young-adult literature, plus change. And the flagged list isn't new books. This year's haul includes Jane Eyre (1847). It includes The Shining (1977) -- Stephen King, pulled 312 times, was the most-banned author in America for the second straight year, an author whose work has sat on school shelves longer than most school boards have existed. The Handmaid's Tale (1985). Speak (1999). Crank (2004). Sold (2006) -- a twenty-year-old National Book Award finalist about child trafficking, and the single most-banned title. Add Tokyo Ghoul manga and you have the full picture: this is backlist. This is the accumulated inventory of American letters, being swept off shelves not because it arrived last Tuesday but because someone finally decided to conduct an inventory review. | | ---|---|--- What actually grew between the quiet 2010s and now is the machinery of removal. State laws that purge by category. Directives that require pulling a book first and reviewing it later. Mass challenges driven by circulating watchlists. And this year's newest tool, confirmed in public records the Texas Freedom to Read Project shared with PEN: school administrators consulting AI chatbots, which recommended removing books -- not because they met any legal standard of obscenity, but, in documented cases, because another district had removed them. Sit with that. A machine in one county clearing a shelf because a machine in another county cleared a shelf. A keyword scanner cannot read Speak and understand it is a novel about the aftermath of rape that a survivor needs to find; it can only see the word. It cannot see that Sold is an argument against the thing it depicts. PEN's Philomena Polefrone put the operating condition plainly: "Confusing and vague state book ban laws and chilling directives from state politicians have created chaos and fear." The AI didn't create the chaos. It industrialized it. To be fair to the supply-side intuition: the catalogue did shift after 2020 -- the CCBC found 51% of children's books it received in 2024 had significant BIPOC content -- and some genuinely explicit material did land in school libraries in that period, to parents' entirely legitimate objection. Curation is not censorship; no student is owed any particular title. And PEN's counting is generous -- a book pulled for a week counts the same as one pulped, which is why the American Library Association's stricter, permanent-removal-only ledger says 5,600. Halve PEN's number. Quarter it. The arithmetic still doesn't reach publishing output, because the books on the shelves haven't changed much in a generation. What changed is what's being done to the shelves. Does it matter? Reading scores are the worst since the test began -- twelfth graders reading at levels not seen in the entire history of the exam, roughly a third of eighth graders below "basic," which is the polite federal word for can't do it -- and the newest national mood is a shrug: does it really matter anyway? It matters, but not the way the press releases say. Not primarily because the economy needs workers, though it does. It matters because reading is the only technology we have for thinking a thought that isn't being streamed to us. A kid who can't read isn't just locked out of Faulkner; he's locked out of the fine print -- the lease, the loan, the ballot measure, the label on the prescription bottle -- which means somebody else will always be happy to explain the world to him, briefly, persuasively, and for a fee. A republic of non-readers becomes a republic of listeners, and listeners get governed by whoever has the loudest feed. The decline took thirty years to register in the data; the consequence doesn't show up in the data at all. It shows up later, in the voting booth and the jury box, when a citizen who was never taught to read deeply has to decide whom to believe -- and picks the confident voice over the true one. So yes. It matters. It's the only score that ever mattered. Reading scores are now the worst in the history of the test -- twelfth graders reading at levels not seen since the exam began, roughly a third of eighth graders below basic, which is the polite federal word for can't do it -- and the newest national mood is a shrug: does it really matter anyway? It matters, but not the way the press releases say. It doesn't matter because the economy needs workers, though it does. It matters because reading is the only technology we have for thinking a thought that isn't being streamed to us. A kid who can't read isn't just locked out of Stephen King; he's locked out of the fine print -- the lease, the loan, the ballot measure, the label on the prescription bottle -- which means someone else will always be happy to explain the world to him, briefly, persuasively, and for a fee. A republic of non-readers is a republic of listeners, and listeners get governed by whoever owns the loudest feed. The score decline took thirty years; the consequence doesn't show up in the data at all. It shows up later, in the voting booth and the jury box, when a citizen who was never taught to read deeply has to decide whom to believe -- and picks the confident voice instead of the true one. So yes. It matters. It may be the only score that ever did. Here is the number that ends the argument: 11,982 bans divided by 7,370 books is 1.6 bans per book. The same titles are being removed, district after district, in bulk, by list, by category, by chatbot. That is not a community reacting to what its libraries contain. That is a process propagating itself. The objectionable-book pipeline the question assumes doesn't exist -- publishers never built anything close to it. You don't need twelve thousand objectionable books a year to get twelve thousand bans. You just need vague laws, circulating lists, and a machine that clears a shelf without ever reading a page -- and someone in the statehouse willing to call that a review. The books weren't the problem. The objections were manufactured at home. This Substack is reader-supported. # The Push to 66!
---
Thousands of miles, countless conversations, and more oil changes than I can count! I've spent the past several months traveling across South Dakota, meeting with folks in communities big and small, and hearing firsthand about the issues that matter most to them.
Now, I'm just a few counties away from visiting all 66 South Dakota counties! I'll be back West River this weekend and heading into central South Dakota next weekend as we work toward that final milestone.
Traveling our state and connecting with South Dakotans has been one of the most rewarding parts of this campaign. Every stop has given me a better understanding of the challenges our communities face and the prorities I'll take with me to Congress.
With less than four weeks until Election Day, we're making our final push to reach as many voters as possible. That means expanding our advertising, getting our message in front of more South Dakotans, and continuing the conversations we've been having across the state.
We've covered a lot of miles, but there's still plenty of work ahead before November 3. Whether you can make a financial contribution, volunteer your time, or both, your support will help us reach more voters and finish this campaign strong.

I'll be back West River this weekend and heading into central South Dakota next weekend as we work toward that final milestone. Traveling our state and connecting with South Dakotans has been one of the most rewarding parts of this campaign. With less than four weeks until Election Day, we're making our final push to reach as many voters as possible. That means expanding our advertising, getting our message in front of more South Dakotans, and continuing the conversations we've been having across the state. # **[OpenAI's $50 billion print just punched a hole in the $852 billion story](https://substack.com/redirect/85ba4356-2dc4-4bfc-86ae-d64e00974aac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
OpenAI told investors it hit roughly $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, not the $68 billion printed last month. The higher figure included partner gross so the lab could sit next to Anthropic,
* **Winners?** Nvidia still sells the shovels, and Anthropic gets the cleaner comp. Anyone short the circular AI complex into this print just got paid. Microsoft's stake is marked, not dead.
* **Losers?** OpenAI's 2027 roadshow, Oracle's $664 billion backlog, and CoreWeave's hostage book. A fresh $30 billion raise on $50 billion of revenue is a harder sale than the $68 billion fairy tale.
* **Next?** Friar calls the lab "very well capitalized" after the $122 billion March round. The $30 billion talks drag, the 2027 debut slips again, and every AI multiple gets recut against $50 billion, not $68 billion.

I called this in **["OpenAI loses another Altman insider before the IPO"](https://substack.com/redirect/095c5b37-ec29-4b63-ac5f-9fafeac1c0b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** on August 11. (Remember those glorious days? When there was gonna be an OpenAI IPO?) Now theres an $852 billion paper empire with no clean roadshow revenue number. Growth of 77% on the run rate and 107% in enterprise is real. It is just not $68 billion. I flagged the **[crack on September 17](https://substack.com/redirect/9f1d1024-4270-40fd-b3ef-67c88d3963ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**. "Confess, Lobby, Delay" A restated top line is the same trick in a spreadsheet. Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave sank because that revenue **IS** the collateral.

# **Trump freezes Microsoft and Adobe green cards and calls it American workers first**
Vance stood up Thursday and froze permanent labor certifications for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Cap Gemini. Since 2009 those names requested almost 3 million foreign workers, took over 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 green-card certifications. Microsoft laid off 6,000 Americans last year and still filed about 6,300 H-1Bs. Vance called it indentured labor. The arithmetic is not subtle.
* **Winners?** American applicants at the wage floor, and shorts in the India body shops. The $100,000 fee on fresh H-1B petitions already raised the price. This freeze kills the green-card path on top of it.
* **Losers?** Microsoft's PERM machine, Adobe's, and the outsourcers who built a business on those 230,000 visas. Nadella took a National Medal of Science the same morning. Honor the CEO. Freeze the conveyor.
* **Next?** No new filings, and pending ones sit. Project Firewall already has about 200 cases. Harvard, Yale and Stanford get the exchange-visa probe next. Microsoft says 80% of its last-year petitions were extensions. Extensions do not refill a laid-off seat.

Washington just priced the indenture. A company that cuts 6,000 Americans and files 6,300 H-1Bs does not get to call that a talent strategy. It is a cost strategy. Cost strategies die when the referee changes. The referee changed Thursday.

# **Britain let Chinese cars in at 10% and Jaecoo just took September**
Britain charges Chinese cars a flat 10% duty. America charges 100%. Europe stacks up to 35.3% on top of 10%. Chinese OEM registrations from January through August hit 519,424, and share went from 12.9% to 28.1%. Hybrids added 62,655 of that, battery-electrics 32,565. **[I already had Jaecoo 7 as the September bestseller on October 5,](https://substack.com/redirect/b63c8114-d33b-40d2-8cc3-2a8cd13d9dcf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** at 10,813 cars. Today's print is 10,814 cars.
* **Winners?** Chery's Jaecoo, BYD and MG, selling a £29,000 ($38,350) Jaecoo 7 against a Discovery Sport at £45,500. The British buyer. Beijing, which just got a showroom the EU tried to close.
* **Losers?** Land Rover, Ford's Puma, and any UK exporter if Reynolds matches the EU levy and China hits back. JLR sells a lot of metal into China. Tariffs travel both ways.
* **Next?** Reynolds is weighing an EU match to dodge the "Made in Europe" rules. The embassy already logged "serious concern" and said it will respond. A BEV-only tariff misses the hybrid wave that actually moved the share.

**[The October 5 call held to the unit.](https://substack.com/redirect/b63c8114-d33b-40d2-8cc3-2a8cd13d9dcf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** Britain invited the volume in, watched share more than double in a year, and is now discovering that Brussels wants the door shut. Match Europe and you tax your own buyer to save an export channel. Stay open and the 28.1% becomes the new floor. There is no free option left on this tape. Much like everything else in Europe, consequences are coming home to roost.

# **Oracle wants Apollo to buy the chips so the debt won 't go on its balance sheet**
Oracle fell 5.22% to $136.07 Thursday and is down nearly 30% this year. It is in talks with Apollo and Goldman to fund a separate company that buys the AI chips, which Oracle then leases. Goal is a deal this year. June-to-August capex was $28.5 billion, against $2.3 billion in that quarter two years ago. Long-term debt has nearly doubled to more than $160 billion. Fifth-largest borrower in the US corporate bond market.
* **Winners?** Apollo and Goldman, if they clip a fee on a shell that keeps the chips off Oracle's books. Nvidia, again, because somebody still has to build the silicon the shell buys.
* **Losers?** ORCL holders, and anyone who thought a $664 billion backlog was cash. OpenAI is one of the biggest customers in that book, and OpenAI's revenue just got marked $20 billion light.
* **Next?** The lease vehicle closes or the bonds cheapen further. Same trick as when Amazon parked Grace Blackwell boxes in an SPV. Credit is the product now. Cloud is the costume.

I **[wrote the spending call](https://substack.com/redirect/64df5e5d-1676-4ece-a521-754e8ef975fa?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/64df5e5d-1676-4ece-a521-754e8ef975fa?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)on July 23, and the **[September 25 Oracle credit tape](https://substack.com/redirect/66a3c42f-3df7-4a3d-8b14-52cea88a42b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/66a3c42f-3df7-4a3d-8b14-52cea88a42b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)already had the bonds and the CDS screaming. A shell that buys the chips so the debt does not hit the parent is not innovation. It is an admission the cash flow cannot carry the build.

# **Nvidia 's Australian data-center IPO just watched the order book die**
Nvidia-backed Firmus Grid, marketed a $5.5 billion listing at A$11 and talked its way to a $30 billion valuation on indications of interest. Days later the book would not clear A$11. Orders closed Thursday with no price and no structure. About 58% of the shares are free to trade from day one. The valuation assumes a pipeline of Asian data centers serving Meta and OpenAI. No track record. Profits years out.
* **Winners?** Anyone who sat out. Public-market buyers just refused to fund another customer-concentrated data-center story at a venture price. That is price discovery, not a glitch.
* **Losers?** Firmus, the early holders staring at a 58% day-one float, and the Nvidia-equity-for-shovels model if this deal gets cut or pulled. Rising borrow costs did the rest.
* **Next?** A price cut, a smaller deal, or a scrap. Wires are already guessing which. If a $30 billion story cannot clear A$11 while OpenAI is restating revenue, the next neocloud IPO does not get a book.

This is the public-market version of the Oracle shell. Nvidia sells the chips, takes the equity, and the customer borrows to buy the chips. That loop worked while the bid was infinite. The bid just flinched.

Whether you're buying equipment, stocking up on inventory, expanding your business, or taking on your next big opportunity, Delta Capital can approve up to $500,000 in business funding in under 5 minutes. And wire the funds within the hour. So if your business is generating $25,000 or more a month, Trump freezes Microsoft and Adobe green cards and calls it American workers first Vance stood up Thursday and froze permanent labor certifications for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Cap Gemini. Since 2009 those names requested almost 3 million foreign workers, took over 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 green-card certifications. Microsoft laid off 6,000 Americans last year and still filed about 6,300 H-1Bs. Vance called it indentured labor. The arithmetic is not subtle. Winners? American applicants at the wage floor, and shorts in the India body shops. The $100,000 fee on fresh H-1B petitions already raised the price. This freeze kills the green-card path on top of it. Losers? Microsoft's PERM machine, Adobe's, and the outsourcers who built a business on those 230,000 visas. Nadella took a National Medal of Science the same morning. Honor the CEO. Freeze the conveyor. Next? No new filings, and pending ones sit. Project Firewall already has about 200 cases. Harvard, Yale and Stanford get the exchange-visa probe next. Microsoft says 80% of its last-year petitions were extensions. Extensions do not refill a laid-off seat. Washington just priced the indenture. A company that cuts 6,000 Americans and files 6,300 H-1Bs does not get to call that a talent strategy. It is a cost strategy. Cost strategies die when the referee changes. The referee changed Thursday. The Capitalist is a reader-supported publication, we exist for you, because of you! Britain let Chinese cars in at 10% and Jaecoo just took September Britain charges Chinese cars a flat 10% duty. America charges 100%. Europe stacks up to 35.3% on top of 10%. Chinese OEM registrations from January through August hit 519,424, and share went from 12.9% to 28.1%. Hybrids added 62,655 of that, battery-electrics 32,565. at 10,813 cars. Today's print is 10,814 cars. Winners? Chery's Jaecoo, BYD and MG, selling a £29,000 ($38,350) Jaecoo 7 against a Discovery Sport at £45,500. The British buyer. Beijing, which just got a showroom the EU tried to close. Losers? Land Rover, Ford's Puma, and any UK exporter if Reynolds matches the EU levy and China hits back. JLR sells a lot of metal into China. Tariffs travel both ways. Next? Reynolds is weighing an EU match to dodge the "Made in Europe" rules. The embassy already logged "serious concern" and said it will respond. A BEV-only tariff misses the hybrid wave that actually moved the share. Britain invited the volume in, watched share more than double in a year, and is now discovering that Brussels wants the door shut. Match Europe and you tax your own buyer to save an export channel. Stay open and the 28.1% becomes the new floor. There is no free option left on this tape. Much like everything else in Europe, consequences are coming home to roost. Oracle wants Apollo to buy the chips so the debt won 't go on its balance sheet Oracle fell 5.22% to $136.07 Thursday and is down nearly 30% this year. It is in talks with Apollo and Goldman to fund a separate company that buys the AI chips, which Oracle then leases. Goal is a deal this year. June-to-August capex was $28.5 billion, against $2.3 billion in that quarter two years ago. Long-term debt has nearly doubled to more than $160 billion. Fifth-largest borrower in the US corporate bond market. Winners? Apollo and Goldman, if they clip a fee on a shell that keeps the chips off Oracle's books. Nvidia, again, because somebody still has to build the silicon the shell buys. Losers? ORCL holders, and anyone who thought a $664 billion backlog was cash. OpenAI is one of the biggest customers in that book, and OpenAI's revenue just got marked $20 billion light. Next? The lease vehicle closes or the bonds cheapen further. Same trick as when Amazon parked Grace Blackwell boxes in an SPV. Credit is the product now. Cloud is the costume. I July 23, and the had the bonds and the CDS screaming. A shell that buys the chips so the debt does not hit the parent is not innovation. It is an admission the cash flow cannot carry the build. Nvidia 's Australian data-center IPO just watched the order book die Nvidia-backed Firmus Grid, marketed a $5.5 billion listing at A$11 and talked its way to a $30 billion valuation on indications of interest. Days later the book would not clear A$11. Orders closed Thursday with no price and no structure. About 58% of the shares are free to trade from day one. The valuation assumes a pipeline of Asian data centers serving Meta and OpenAI. No track record. Profits years out. Winners? Anyone who sat out. Public-market buyers just refused to fund another customer-concentrated data-center story at a venture price. That is price discovery, not a glitch. Losers? Firmus, the early holders staring at a 58% day-one float, and the Nvidia-equity-for-shovels model if this deal gets cut or pulled. Rising borrow costs did the rest. Next? A price cut, a smaller deal, or a scrap. Wires are already guessing which. If a $30 billion story cannot clear A$11 while OpenAI is restating revenue, the next neocloud IPO does not get a book. This is the public-market version of the Oracle shell. Nvidia sells the chips, takes the equity, and the customer borrows to buy the chips. That loop worked while the bid was infinite. The bid just flinched. That's the tape OpenAI's collateral got marked from $68 billion to $50 billion, and Oracle answered by trying to lease the chips off the books. Firmus just proved that the public appetite for that loop is no longer bottomless. Britain doubled Chinese car share to 28.1% at a 10% duty and is now stuck between Brussels and Beijing. _Story by Rachid Mohsen*_
SANA'A, Yemen--On the afternoon of October 5, 14-year-old Athir al-Amri had just taken the last exam of her first semester. She was on a school bus going home when an airstrike hit next to the bus as it drove through the Saawan area of eastern Sana'a, Yemen's capital. Shrapnel struck her in the head, killing her, witnesses and relatives said.
"She was planning to spend the holiday playing as all children do during school breaks," her 35-year-old cousin, Mohammed Al-Lahida, told Drop Site News. "The shrapnel decapitated her. If her mother saw her body, she would die of grief."
Two of her classmates were also wounded, one of them gravely, in the strike by the Saudi-led coalition.
Ansarallah, an armed group also known as the Houthis, seized the capital Sana'a in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 on the side of Yemen's internationally recognized government. A civil war raged for eight years, killing tens of thousands and sparking one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, until a fragile ceasefire was brokered in 2022.
The civil war reignited in July when Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes to prevent an inbound Iranian passenger plane from landing in Ansarallah-controlled Sana'a. In response, Ansarallah declared a maritime blockade on all Saudi-linked vessels in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
The fighting escalated sharply last month when Ansarallah swept down the Red Sea coast, overcoming Saudi-backed government forces and capturing the key port city of Mokha as well as islands in the Bab el-Mandab Strait, allowing them to tighten their declared blockade of Saudi shipping. Saudi Arabia and its allied forces in Yemen then embarked on a military offensive to retake the territory, launching airstrikes on Ansarallah along the Red Sea coast and other areas controlled by the group, including Sana'a. Ansarallah responded by escalating missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition's Colonel Turki Al-Maliki [said on October 5](https://substack.com/redirect/bc208747-2929-40c8-a1c4-663f54cea5c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that 100 fighter jets took part in [Operation Dawn of Yemen](https://substack.com/redirect/d7568bd7-cc45-40b5-a8d9-9a8278e41530?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and destroyed 324 "high-value targets," including weapons depots, boat explosives storage and naval mines. He described them as "legitimate military targets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia."
Brigadier General Yahya Saree [said on X ](https://substack.com/redirect/be4c1415-d3d0-42a6-85c3-5e9de70bd2ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)on October 7 that the Saudi coalition had carried out 1,798 airstrikes and missile attacks since the escalation began, concentrated on Sanaa, Taiz, Marib, and Al-Jawf. On October 6 and 7, Ansarallah [fired ballistic missiles](https://substack.com/redirect/16141201-111c-4a3f-9696-190e361f95af?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) at Abha International Airport in Saudi Arabia's Asir region and at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing three people, wounding dozens, and disrupting operations, the coalition said, [accusing](https://substack.com/redirect/8eccd45e-17c3-4c9a-aefc-84ac2d650a65?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the Houthis of "terrorist attacks on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom."
Almost 1,000 people have been killed in the latest fighting, most of them fighters, with over 200,000 displaced, according to the United Nations. Al-Amri is among 83 civilians killed and 146 wounded in Ansarallah-controlled areas since the escalation began in September, Dr. Anees Al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Ansarallah health ministry, told Drop Site News, around 60% of them women and children.
## **" Shrapnel tore through the vehicle"**
Rehab Al-Jaafari and Reem Al-Wakedi, both also 14 years old, were on the bus with al-Amri. Al-Jaafari's father, Bassem, told Drop Site News they were the only three girls left on the bus when the strike happened. Al-Jaafari told her father they had asked the driver to stop and wait when the first missile hit near the Atiya petrol station nearby.
"He told them not to worry and sped on to reach safety. As the bus passed a Houthi compound that was being targeted, a second missile struck and shrapnel tore through the vehicle. Rehab pulled the classmate beside her down beneath the seat. Athir was sitting in the back row," the father said.
Al-Jaafari woke up later in the back of a Houthi military pickup truck, one of several military vehicles that carried the wounded to Al-Nubala Hospital. Al-Wakedi sustained moderate injuries to her arm and was in the emergency room having her wounds dressed. Before she went into intensive care, Al-Jaafari asked her father where the other girls were. Bassem told his daughter that al-Amri was being treated on another floor. He did not tell her she had been killed.
Al-Jaafari had shrapnel lodged in her back and lost the sight in her right eye. A wound to her face damaged her ear and left her unable to open her mouth properly. She remains on intravenous fluids and is vomiting whatever she eats. Doctors removed shrapnel from her right arm, and a wound to her right foot means it will be some time before she can walk. The hospital discharged her on October 6, according to her father, though she requires continued medical care.
## **No Shelter**
On October 3, a strike near al-Sabeen Hospital for Maternity and Childhood in Sana'a [damaged](https://substack.com/redirect/b65cf325-d352-4d66-a90e-31daeb741fe6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the facility's windows, medical equipment, and medicine supplies, and injured 10 staff and patients, the health ministry's Al-Asbahi told Drop Site.
A nurse, Aisha Mohammed, said her right arm was broken when a door fell on her. Window glass shattered and breathing equipment flew across the room. "Premature babies and infants in incubators were among the most exposed," Mohammed said. The next day, on October 6, warplanes flew over again, causing some patients to flee the hospital.
Only about 60% of Yemen's health facilities are fully functioning, and comprehensive trauma and emergency care is available at about 6% of those assessed, [according](https://substack.com/redirect/98f6b758-e42b-4d3f-b22c-d3b472447cf0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to the World Health Organization (WHO).
"Our hospitals cannot withstand this kind of attack," Al-Asbahi said, warning that hospitals rely on generators that need scarce fuel.
Residents say the launch of ballistic missiles from inside the city brings its own terror. At dawn on October 8, people woke to a huge blast that many thought was a strike. It was a missile launched from near Sana'a airport, residents said.
Wesam Ahmed, who works for a company delivering goods from Jeddah--Saudi Arabia's second-largest city--to Sana'a, said strikes damaged its office in Attan, southwest of Sana'a. He said he has suspended work and lost hundreds of customers.
Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the Geneva-based SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, which documents violations in Yemen, said the Saudi-led strikes have hit populated areas in broad daylight. The internationally recognized government has [warned](https://substack.com/redirect/2cdb5f73-2b9b-4302-be1f-c8c47faead10?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) residents to stay away from Ansarallah military sites.
"But in Sana'a, avoiding every site linked to the group could mean avoiding large parts of the city, which has no civil defense system or shelters to speak of," al-Hamidi said.

The Saudi-led coalition's Colonel Turki Al-Maliki that 100 fighter jets took part in and destroyed 324 "high-value targets," including weapons depots, boat explosives storage and naval mines. He described them as "legitimate military targets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia." Brigadier General Yahya Saree October 7 that the Saudi coalition had carried out 1,798 airstrikes and missile attacks since the escalation began, concentrated on Sanaa, Taiz, Marib, and Al-Jawf. On October 6 and 7, Ansarallah at Abha International Airport in Saudi Arabia's Asir region and at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing three people, wounding dozens, and disrupting operations, the coalition said, the Houthis of "terrorist attacks on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom." Almost 1,000 people have been killed in the latest fighting, most of them fighters, with over 200,000 displaced, according to the United Nations. Al-Amri is among 83 civilians killed and 146 wounded in Ansarallah-controlled areas since the escalation began in September, Dr. Anees Al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Ansarallah health ministry, told Drop Site News, around 60% of them women and children. " Shrapnel tore through the vehicle" Rehab Al-Jaafari and Reem Al-Wakedi, both also 14 years old, were on the bus with al-Amri. Al-Jaafari's father, Bassem, told Drop Site News they were the only three girls left on the bus when the strike happened. Al-Jaafari told her father they had asked the driver to stop and wait when the first missile hit near the Atiya petrol station nearby. "He told them not to worry and sped on to reach safety. As the bus passed a Houthi compound that was being targeted, a second missile struck and shrapnel tore through the vehicle. Rehab pulled the classmate beside her down beneath the seat. Athir was sitting in the back row," the father said. Al-Jaafari woke up later in the back of a Houthi military pickup truck, one of several military vehicles that carried the wounded to Al-Nubala Hospital. Al-Wakedi sustained moderate injuries to her arm and was in the emergency room having her wounds dressed. Before she went into intensive care, Al-Jaafari asked her father where the other girls were. Bassem told his daughter that al-Amri was being treated on another floor. He did not tell her she had been killed. Al-Jaafari had shrapnel lodged in her back and lost the sight in her right eye. A wound to her face damaged her ear and left her unable to open her mouth properly. She remains on intravenous fluids and is vomiting whatever she eats. Doctors removed shrapnel from her right arm, and a wound to her right foot means it will be some time before she can walk. The hospital discharged her on October 6, according to her father, though she requires continued medical care. No Shelter On October 3, a strike near al-Sabeen Hospital for Maternity and Childhood in Sana'a the facility's windows, medical equipment, and medicine supplies, and injured 10 staff and patients, the health ministry's Al-Asbahi told Drop Site. A nurse, Aisha Mohammed, said her right arm was broken when a door fell on her. Window glass shattered and breathing equipment flew across the room. "Premature babies and infants in incubators were among the most exposed," Mohammed said. The next day, on October 6, warplanes flew over again, causing some patients to flee the hospital. Only about 60% of Yemen's health facilities are fully functioning, and comprehensive trauma and emergency care is available at about 6% of those assessed, to the World Health Organization (WHO). "Our hospitals cannot withstand this kind of attack," Al-Asbahi said, warning that hospitals rely on generators that need scarce fuel. Residents say the launch of ballistic missiles from inside the city brings its own terror. At dawn on October 8, people woke to a huge blast that many thought was a strike. It was a missile launched from near Sana'a airport, residents said. Wesam Ahmed, who works for a company delivering goods from Jeddah--Saudi Arabia's second-largest city--to Sana'a, said strikes damaged its office in Attan, southwest of Sana'a. He said he has suspended work and lost hundreds of customers. Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the Geneva-based SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, which documents violations in Yemen, said the Saudi-led strikes have hit populated areas in broad daylight. The internationally recognized government has residents to stay away from Ansarallah military sites. "But in Sana'a, avoiding every site linked to the group could mean avoiding large parts of the city, which has no civil defense system or shelters to speak of," al-Hamidi said. The reporter has been granted anonymity because of the security situation in Yemen. Rachid Mohsen is a pseudonym. name: Jim Schultz
subject: Three years later, we must continue to remember Oct. 7
body:
Three years ago, Hamas-led terrorists murdered nearly 1,200 people in Israel & raped & brutalized countless women. The stories from that day are pain

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/ab8a8a3d5a38/the-briefing-from-mpbc-13063185?e=baf210d431)

| | | | |

| |

Three years ago, Hamas-led terrorists murdered nearly 1,200 people in Israel and raped and brutalized countless women. The stories from that day are painful to revisit: a nine-month-old shot dead in her mother's arms, a father killed in front of his two young sons. But we owe the victims the honesty of remembering what was done to them. Some have tried to explain the attackers' motives as a product of poverty or mistreatment. That is absurd. Millions endure poverty, repression and war without murdering their neighbors. Treating atrocity as a predictable response to hardship insults those who suffer, and it shifts our attention from the victims to the grievances of their killers. The responsibility rests with the perpetrators and the institutions that taught them to hate. The hatred behind Oct. 7 is not confined to the Middle East. Here in America, Israeli embassy employees were gunned down outside a Jewish museum in Washington. An attack in Boulder on people advocating for hostages ultimately killed an 82-year-old woman. This March, an attacker rammed a vehicle into a Michigan synagogue with 140 children inside. Antisemitic assaults, vandalism and harassment hit a 46-year high in 2024, and every synagogue, Jewish school and community center now has to plan for its own security. No other religious or ethnic group in America faces threats like these. Worse, antisemitism is being mainstreamed in our politics and culture, from both the left and the right. Those of us who are not Jewish need to stand in solidarity with the Jewish people. Our Jewish friends and neighbors should not have to guess where we stand. That is the argument I made in the _Star Tribune_ yesterday, and I hope you'll read it. [**Read "Three years later, we must continue to remember Oct. 7" here.** ](https://us.list-manage.com/11PY5nuGi7U?e=baf210d431&c2id=93c61d534406ea5269257c101c1d1f83)

That's less than $10 a month to be part of the organized private-sector counterweight this state desperately needs — at the exact moment it needs it most. | FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
---
| Release Date: October 8, 2026
---
| Forlini Dominates Secretary of State Debate With Experience and Reliability Making the Difference
---
The Contrast Was Clear
---
| Ann Arbor, Mich: Anthony Forlini decisively won the Secretary of State Debate this evening on the campus of the University of Michigan at the Ford School of Public Policy.
Anthony Forlini commented, "I was glad to highlight what matters most to Michigan citizens - having someone who will be transparent, experienced, reliable and committed to removing politics out of the office. This debate gave a clear contrast of the strengths I bring to the table, particularly compared to my opponent."
Forlini and his opponent gathered at the Ford School of Public Policy in a debate hosted and coordinated by the University. Their energetic discussion lasted just an hour in front of a full auditorium and an overflow room with many others joining from around the state online.
Various topics were covered from elections to data management to safety and security. Forlini highlighted the importance of transparency, reliability, and the need to move politics out of the office and focus just on serving the citizens of Michigan in a non-partisan manner.
The Lt. Governor attempted to connect Forlini to issues he has had nothing to do through half-truths and innuendo, attempting to make connections that simply do not exist.
Forlini noted, "It was interesting to see how the Lt. Governor forgot he has been #2 in charge of Michigan for over 7.5 years. He talked about a number of things that should be done, but he clearly could have had an impact on these things while he has been Lt. Governor. Instead, he hasn't taken his job seriously. He only made it to Senate session 6% of the time last year - a 94% absentee rate. It's safe to assume he will not take the role of Secretary of State seriously either if elected because how you do anything is how you do everything."
He concluded, "I am running because as a current Clerk, I understand what the job entails. My team and I have found solutions that I want to the state of Michigan. I've been there and done that and am ready to make an impact on Day 1. And I'll be there, every day, for Michigan."

body:
New ad highlights rising flood insurance premiums and Letlow’s commitment to holding FEMA and insurance companies accountable

| | |
---

| | | | | | FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASEOctober 8, 2026katherine@julialetlow.com
**JULIA LETLOW RELEASES NEW AD TAKING ON SOARING FLOOD INSURANCE COSTS IN LOUISIANA** _New ad highlights rising flood insurance premiums and Letlow’s commitment to holding FEMA and insurance companies accountable_
**BATON ROUGE, LA** — Congresswoman Julia Letlow, the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in Louisiana, released a new campaign ad focused on the rising cost of flood insurance in Louisiana and her commitment to holding FEMA and major insurance companies accountable for bringing costs down for Louisiana families.
In the ad, Letlow highlights how flood insurance premiums have increased by as much as 200%, placing an enormous financial burden on homeowners and threatening to price families out of their homes and out of Louisiana altogether.
_“Louisiana families should not have to worry about being priced out of their own homes because of skyrocketing flood insurance premiums,”_**said Congresswoman Julia Letlow.** _“I've fought to protect Louisiana homeowners in Congress, and in the Senate, I'll continue holding FEMA and big insurance companies accountable, demanding transparency, and working to bring these costs down.”_
Letlow has made flood insurance affordability a priority during her time in Congress, including co-sponsoring legislation to prevent lapses in the National Flood Insurance Program. She has also advocated for greater transparency in FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 methodology and long-term reforms to make flood insurance more affordable and accessible.
The new ad underscores Letlow's commitment to protecting Louisiana homeowners and ensuring families can afford to remain in the communities they call home.
**WATCH THE AD HERE:**

---](https://us.list-manage.com/12VGsKv7hBk?e=95355a072c&c2id=cd64ea42b1b0eeac0fd7d107db75288a)
| | | | | | **TRANSCRIPT:**
JULIA LETLOW: _I’m Julia Letlow._
_Here in Louisiana, we know being flooded is a tragedy._
_And for many, it’s the first of two tragedies._
_Flood insurance has gone up 200%._
_It’s so expensive now, our seniors have to sell the homes that they paid off._
_That’s unconscionable._
_I’m holding FEMA and the big insurance companies accountable to lower costs._
_And I won’t stop until they do._
_I’m Julia Letlow and I approve this message._

clean_body: I'm proud to deliver this deal for New Mexicans. I'm thrilled to share the news: We just secured a major deal to lower energy costs, create good-paying jobs, and protect New Mexico families and small businesses from being stuck with the costs of massive new data centers. Data centers use enormous amounts of electricity — and connecting them to the grid and building the infrastructure they need can be incredibly expensive. This deal makes data centers pay those costs themselves, instead of passing the bill on to New Mexicans. It will also help get clean energy connected to the grid faster. That will mean new job opportunities in clean energy, manufacturing, and infrastructure across New Mexico. And we’re doing it while protecting the places that make our state so special. We kept key environmental and consultation safeguards in place, protected the public’s ability to challenge projects, and secured dedicated funding to clean up abandoned hardrock mines. I’ve always believed we can lower costs, create good jobs, and protect our public lands at the same time. I'm proud to deliver a deal that makes this possible. Artificial intelligence is changing everything – how we work, how we learn, how we get our news, how decisions get made about our lives. That's not a future prediction. It's happening right now.

| | | | Hi Friend,
Every politician says they're against waste, fraud, and abuse. So let's look at how Suhas Subramanyam voted.
In June, the House passed the Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act, which lets agencies pause payments when there are clear signs of fraud. Suhas voted no.
In September, the House passed the National Fraud Enforcement Division Act, which creates a permanent fraud division at the Department of Justice. It passed 352 to 72, with 139 Democrats voting yes. **Suhas was one of the 72 who voted no.**
The same day, the House passed the PROOF Act, which requires states to share data so investigators can catch fraud in programs like Medicaid, SNAP, and TANF. **Suhas voted no again.**
**Stopping fraud should not be a hard vote.**
Every stolen dollar is a dollar that should have gone to the people these programs are meant to help, and it adds to a debt our kids will inherit.
As a 30-year Air Force veteran and former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense, **I know the importance of accountability.**
And I believe our elected officials must be held accountable for their spending decisions and the consequences those decisions have for Virginia families.
But I can’t do it alone.
_I need your support to defeat Suhas Subramanyam, expose his voting record, and make fiscal responsibility a priority once more in Congress._

| | | Our federal government continues spending more than it takes in, leaving our children and grandchildren to shoulder the debt. I'm a father, and I want my kids to inherit opportunity, not a mountain of debt.
When I get to Congress, I will vote to protect your tax dollars.
My plan calls for disciplined spending, cutting waste, fraud, and abuse, and ending Washington's perpetual deficits.
Virginia families have to live within their means. Washington should too.
**It's time to restore faith in the American Dream.**
God bless, Dave Beckwith
**Beckwith for Congress** _Restoring Faith in the American Dream_

You are being fed a diet of finished conclusions.
Every day, a thousand voices--pundits, campaign advertisements, political organizations, and curated news feeds--offer you a version of reality that feels complete. They tell you what happened, who is responsible, what a candidate believes, and what you should think about it.
The work of citizenship begins when you decide to look for yourself.
We the People did not surrender political judgment when we elected representatives. A vote authorizes someone to exercise public authority; it does not transfer our responsibility to understand what that authority is being used to do.
That does not mean you must know everything. It means that when something matters, you know how to proceed.
## It Starts With a Lead
Consider a candidate running for governor.
In 2025, Byron Donalds spoke favorably about the growth of data centers in Florida, describing the power demands as critical and arguing that Florida should embrace the opportunity rather than run away from it. Then the landscape changed.
In May 2026, a Change Research survey of 1,593 likely Florida voters found that 79 percent opposed AI data centers. In July, H.R. 9777--the Protecting Ratepayers Act--was introduced in Congress. The proposal would require large data centers to provide their own off-grid power and water rather than shifting those infrastructure costs to the public. Florida had also enacted SB 484, establishing requirements for large-load customers and addressing ratepayer costs and water permitting.
Now there was something worth investigating.
Not because a poll proves a candidate wrong. Not because a new bill proves a candidate changed. And not because a campaign statement tells us what the government can actually do.
The question is: **What does the record actually show?**
## Follow the Question
The first step is to separate the pieces. What did the candidate actually say? When did he say it? What happened afterward? What did the government actually do? What authority belongs to the office being sought?
Those questions matter because political language and government action are not the same thing. A candidate can support a policy without having the authority to enact it. A law can exist without proving that a particular candidate caused it. A federal proposal can be politically relevant to a gubernatorial campaign without being an action available to a governor.
So the record must be followed before the judgment is made.
This is where the work changes. You are no longer asking, _" What am I being told about this candidate?"_ You are asking, _" What have I established about this candidate?"_
## Do Not Fill the Gap
The temptation comes when the record leaves a space.
Donalds's earlier position on data centers was clear. The later record showed a more restrictive policy direction. But the record did not establish why the change occurred.
Perhaps the candidate's position changed. Perhaps the policy became more specific. Perhaps the political circumstances changed. Perhaps the candidate always intended something different from what the earlier statement suggested.
The evidence does not answer that question.
So we do not fill the gap.
That is one of the most important disciplines in citizen investigation: **An unanswered question is not permission to invent an answer.**
The same discipline applies when the subject is law, regulation, authority, or political motive.
## The Second Lead
The same candidate offered another opportunity to test the method.
In July 2026, Donalds called for a "full and immediate pause" on Flock and similar automated license plate reader systems, raising constitutional and privacy concerns and warning against a surveillance state.
After the Florida Sheriffs Association responded, his position moved toward working with sheriffs and police chiefs to establish parameters and limitations rather than maintaining an outright pause.
Again, the sequence can be established. Again, the explanation cannot simply be assumed.
And again, the question of authority matters. Who controls the use of these systems? What authority belongs to the governor? What belongs to sheriffs? What belongs to police chiefs, counties, municipalities, or state agencies?
In August, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked general-use permits for automated license plate readers in state highway rights-of-way.
That is a government action. It is evidence. But it is not automatically evidence of gubernatorial control.
The work is to follow the authority to its source.
## When the Record Does Not Give You a Label
You may reach the end of an investigation without a satisfying political label. You may not be able to prove that a candidate is a "flip-flopper." You may not be able to prove that a candidate was acting from political calculation. You may not be able to prove that a campaign promise will become government action.
That is not failure. It is an honest finding.
A disciplined citizen can say: _This is established. This is supported by the record. This is contradicted. This remains unresolved._
And then make a judgment.
The point of investigation is not to manufacture certainty. It is to make your judgment answerable to what you can actually establish.
## The Vote Is Still Yours
Eventually, investigation reaches a point where evidence gives way to judgment.
That is the purpose of the work. You decide what matters to you. You decide how much uncertainty you are willing to accept. You decide what a candidate's record means in relation to the American Kitchen Table--your family's freedom, security, prosperity, and future.
Before you make that decision, ask one more question: **What remaining fact or contradiction could actually change my judgment?**
If there is one, investigate it. If there is not, you may be ready to decide.
The judgment is yours.
## The Election Is Not the End
A vote does not end citizenship.
If the candidate you supported wins, the promise still has to become practice. If the candidate you opposed wins, the government still belongs to you.
Watch what happens next. Watch the laws, the budgets, the votes, the appointments, the administrative actions, public statements, reports, and the decisions that follow. Compare what was promised with what is being done.
When something changes, begin again.
A new matter becomes a new question. A new question begins the work again.
**DECODE. AUDIT. STRIKE. SECURE.**
That is how accountability becomes a continuing practice rather than an election-season event.
## Political Sovereignty
Political sovereignty is not freedom from influence. It is not distrusting everyone. It is not investigating everything. It is accepting responsibility for your own political judgment.
You can listen to experts. You can read journalism. You can use voter guides. You can listen to candidates and people you trust. But you should know what you are trusting, why you are trusting it, and when something matters enough to look further.
That is the difference between receiving a conclusion and possessing the means to examine one.
The citizen comes first.
## Bring It Back to the Kitchen Table
The work eventually returns to the place where politics becomes real: the American Kitchen Table.
Not the campaign stage. Not the television panel. Not the social-media argument.
The table where people think about their families, their work, their homes, their communities, their freedom, their security, and the future they are leaving behind.
The question is simple: **Does this make the family at the American Kitchen Table more free, secure, and prosperous?**
That is not a slogan. It is a measure. And the citizen is the one who must apply it.
## The Work Continues
The full **Citizen 's Candidate Investigation Manual** takes this work further, providing the complete method, procedures, evidence practices, worksheets, and working examples.
It will be available free to American Kitchen Table Founding Members.
The link to the Manual will be posted here shortly.
You do not need to know everything before you begin. You only need to notice when something matters, ask the next question, and do the next thing the matter requires.
The citizen comes first. The responsibility remains. The work continues.
**DECODE. AUDIT. STRIKE. SECURE.**
**Strike the Root. Secure the Table.**
